Course Descriptions

Please select the course ID below to view the course descriptions.

IB 540 - Encuentros y Descencuentros: Temas en Etica Social
Este curso tiene como objetivo primario la centralización de principios éticos que orientan nuestro quehacer sociocultural, político, religioso y comunitario a la búsqueda intencional de la equidad, la justicia y la libertad. Al referirnos a lo político, no aludimos a la política partidista, sino a su definición fundamental como el poder del pueblo o del ciudadano, y por lo tanto, a cómo se ejerce el poder de manera responsable dentro del polis, es decir, en la vida colectiva del pueblo y la comunidad. La meta es generar un espacio para discutir los retos y oportunidades de la ética social en nuestros contextos, analizando nuestras prácticas y su relación con el paradigma de los derechos humanos y con nuestro quehacer teológico. Este curso aportará al desarrollo de las competencias socio-políticas necesarias para un ministerio audaz y capaz de prestar servicios esenciales a la comunidad.


Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Alexandra Rosado-Roman
IB 541 - Troubles and Tears: Ethcial Questions Facing the African American Church
The Black community is not a monolithic. Yet, while a diverse group, they share a history of pain and trauma that arises from historical oppressions and structural sins such as racism, sexism, homophobia, and economic discrimination. This course will examine the ethical questions that arise from the perspective of those who have been historically subjected to trauma and how the Church can be an ally in their search for justice.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Sharon Ellis Davis
IB 551 – Ethical Forms
This course in theological ethics will focus moral frameworks as tools for making moral judgments. The course will begin by focusing on the role of scripture, tradition, reason and experience in ethical decision making and will then move to an exploration of different frameworks and sources such as Natural Law, Virtue ethics, Narrative ethics, Responsibility/American Empirical Theology and ethics, and feminist and liberationist approaches.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0 (Offered Online or during On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Dr. Chris Rodkey
IB 552 – God and Science: Intro Biomedical Ethics
This course in theological ethics will focus on biomedical ethics (sometimes called bioethics). Students will be introduced to methods within bioethics as tools for making moral judgments. The course will begin by focusing on a description of bioethics and then turn to a case study that focus on 1) access to healthcare and 2) life at its beginnings.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0 (Offered Online or during On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Dr. Chris Rodkey
IB 553 – Social Ethics
This course introduces the theory and method of Social Ethics and considers how the issues and applications of social ethics influence both the local church and the wider society. Using case studies to examine specific theoretical and practical issues, we will exercise our own ideas and applications of social ethics. The aim, of course, is neither to answer every question nor to justify particular stances but, rather, to learn to ask relevant questions, to understand how ethical decisions correspond to theological belief, to communicate clearly one’s own ethical values, and to expand understandings of diverse worldviews. Students will be encouraged to develop their analytical and critical thinking skills, to reflect on their own processes of ethical reflection, and to communicate their ideas in articulate ways

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christy Newton
IB 554 – Living the Catholic Experience: Ethics and Social Justice
This course introduces the Catholic tradition of social justice, tracing its historical development and the seven guiding principles rooted in Scripture, papal encyclicals, and Church teaching. Students will explore how these principles shape Gospel living and apply them locally in Kentucky and globally. Through stories, reflection, and discussion, participants will connect theory to practice by examining lived experiences of justice and considering their own role in building a more just world.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Jean Soto
IB 555 – An Introduction to Faith Rooted Anti-Racism
This course will provide an introductory survey of faith-rooted approaches to anti-racism, and anti-racist community practices. It will explore practical approaches to resisting racism, and to communication, accountability and listening across difference to create a more just church in a just society through systemic analysis coupled with contextual learning and dynamic interaction. Race, justice, identity formation, power, and intersectionality will be considered alongside tools to address racism, and other forms of oppression to increase equity and meaningful social change.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Rev. Dr. Don Gillett, II
IB 556 – Ethical Leadership in Extraordinary Times
This two-week, half-credit course equips Christian leaders to respond ethically to urgent social challenges—from pandemics and climate change to racial injustice and political polarization. Through case studies, personal narratives, and theological reflection, students will explore frameworks for ethical leadership that engage both inner spirituality and public responsibility. The course emphasizes moving beyond disengagement to cultivate moral voices that address injustice with clarity, courage, and compassion.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Sharon Ellis Davis
IB 557 – Green Sex (is Beautiful)
This course explores the intersection of sexual ethics, spirituality, and ecological responsibility through Pope Francis’ Laudato si’. Students will examine how intimate relationships and care for the earth are deeply connected, reflecting on how healing human relationships contributes to environmental restoration. Through readings, discussions, and a creative final project, participants will discover how harmonizing earth-care with just and loving sexual living becomes a theological “way of beauty.”

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Jean Soto
IB 558 - Food Injustice Cohort
This class explores issues of food justice from the perspective of Christian Social Ethics, which begins from the insights of people’s movements and everyday life. This rooted approach is coupled with an exploration of the constructive role that the prophetic imagination and the social teachings of Jesus Christ can play in guiding our ministries and communities. In addition to course readings and discussion, students will engage in various mapping exercises to gain greater understanding of how the needs of their community, wider social efforts, and ministries of the church relate to each other—both in terms of fruitful cooperation and deeper power dynamics. These elements fit together as a process of discernment to determine the kinds of relationships, spiritual exercises, and partnerships that deepen and expand current food related ministries to be more justice-oriented over time.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Wilson Dickinson
IB 559 - Decolonizing Ministry: Pastoral Practice in a Colonized World
This course explores how Christian ministry is shaped by the enduring realities of colonial power and its effects on communities, identities, and spiritual life. Using the thought of Frantz Fanon as a central guide, students will examine how colonial systems have influenced the psyche, social relationships, and structures of belonging, and how these dynamics continue to affect pastoral contexts today. The course also explores constructive pastoral responses. Drawing on decolonial perspectives, students will consider how ministry can foster healing, restore dignity, and cultivate communities rooted in justice, mutual recognition, and liberation. By engaging Fanon’s insights alongside practical ministry reflection, participants will develop pastoral approaches capable of responding faithfully to a world still shaped by colonial histories and committed to restoring relationships among people, communities, and God.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Alexandra Rosado Roman
IB 569 – Technology as a New Form of Sacred
This course explores technology as more than tools—examining it as a pervasive paradigm shaping life and faith in the 21st century. Students will engage philosophical and theological perspectives on the “technocratic paradigm” and consider Christian responses to technology’s power and influence. Through readings, discussions, and online presentations, participants will critically reflect on technology’s ethical and spiritual implications and develop frameworks for faithful engagement in a tech-driven world.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
IB 570 – Globalization and the Local Church
Although many people in local churches today find it difficult to define globalization, there is no doubt that the processes of globalization affect each one of our lives. Globalization is complex, fragmented, and contradictorily-understood, but ultimately, globalization is about local and global relationships. This course challenges students to reflect critically upon the ethical and spiritual ramifications of globalization and to consider practical ways to respond to it within the life of local congregations. Through readings, discussion forums, online presentations, and a writing project, we will develop and apply understandings of the relationship between globalization and the daily life of faith.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Christy Newton
IB 573 – Church, Society and the Ethics of Global Warming
The natural environments that sustain life on earth are built entirely upon and within social relationships. And for this important reason, both church and society are implicated in the causes and consequences of global warming. In this course, we will consider questions about the fragility and resiliency of the planet, consumption and the global market empire, environmental justice and environmental racism, and the importance of exercising moral agency. We will examine the ethical responsibilities we have to our natural environments as people of faith and members of global society. Through readings, videos, discussion forums, online presentations, and a writing project, we will deepen our understanding of climate change from the context of faith and seek to reconcile the ethical disconnect between human and environmental well-being.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Christy Newton
IB 574 – Black Lives Matter: Issues of Race and Ethics for Church Leaders
How do the resources and tools of Christian social ethics shape our understanding and experience of the Black Lives Matter movement? This movement brings with it specific ethical concerns and ethical responsibilities for all people of faith. And as a church that aims to become anti-racist and pro-reconciling, these concerns and responsibilities are especially poignant. This course challenges students to reflect critically upon the ethical and spiritual ramifications of the Black Lives Matter movement in light of our understandings of the common good, personal experience, tradition, faith, reason, and social sin. Through readings, videos, discussion forums, online presentations, and a writing project, we will develop practical, ethical, faithful responses to Black Lives Matter.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Christy Newton
IB 578 – Public Theology and the Common Good
Many people believe that our theological and religious beliefs should be kept private. However, these beliefs and the ethical practices they motivate inevitably shape our understandings of the roles and purposes of public life and public policy. In reality, even our “private” beliefs produce public outcomes. This course challenges students to reflect critically on the meaning and purpose of the common good, the ways public theologies are formulated and expressed, and the role public theologies have in advocating for the common good. Through readings, videos, online presentations, discussion forums, and a writing project, we will consider reasons and ways moral language is used in the public sphere and how it might be employed to further the common good.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Christy Newton
IB 582 – Clergy Wellness / Boundaries
This two-week online course equips clergy to establish and maintain healthy boundaries for effective pastoral leadership. Students will explore strategies for clergy wellness, identify boundary violations—including sexual misconduct, gender discrimination, and burnout—and develop practices for self-care. Through readings, discussions, and reflection, participants will learn how healthy boundaries foster authentic ministry and congregational health across diverse contexts.

While this course is also intended to help students and clergy meet standing requirements regarding healthy boundaries in ministry, PLEASE CONFIRM THAT YOUR JUDICATORY WILL ACCEPT THIS COURSE AS APPROPRIATE TO MEET THAT REQUIREMENT.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Yvonne Martinez Thorne
IB 583 – The Church’s Challenge to Become Anti-Racist: From Theory to Action
This course will invite students to engage in the critical thinking process about the nature of ecclesia and faith, the spiritual roots of anti-racism, the church’s call for prophetic embodiment, and practical approaches to implement transformation and reconciliation. Through readings, discussion, and online presentations from the instructor, students will be invited to develop an action plan to advance the ministry of anti-racism and inclusion in their congregations and faith bodies.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
IB 584 – Ecowomanism and Environmental Justice
This course examines environmental injustice through theological and ethical lenses, focusing on Christian responses and ecowomanism as a framework for justice. Students will explore root causes of environmental harm and assess faith-based approaches to dismantling it. Through readings, films, podcasts, and a progressive Eco-justice Proposal, participants will integrate ecowomanist principles into ministerial or denominational contexts, developing practical strategies for addressing ecological and social inequities.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
IB 585 – Is a Migrant my Neighbor - The Church's Response
Many social and political tensions arise around the treatment of non-citizens. We open an investigation of our sacred Scriptures seeking the light of divine wisdom for a Gospel response to the complex immigration circumstances of our time. In this course we enquire into the important Old Testament theme of “migrant”, delve into the meaning of “neighbor” in the New Testament, and discover the migrant within ourselves as followers of Jesus.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Wasoian
IB 590 -IB Competency Exercise
*Please refer to section 7.1.6-7.1.8 of the Student Handbook*

Prerequisite: Completion of all other IB 500 level work
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Kristel Clayville
IB 672 -“Want Fries with That?”: Cultural Globalization, Economic Ethics and Church Life
This course explores the intersection of religion, globalization, and economics, examining how faith traditions have shaped—and been shaped by—global systems. Students will critically reflect on the ethical and spiritual implications of cultural and economic globalization and consider practical responses for individuals and congregations. Through readings, multimedia resources, discussions, and a writing project, participants will engage topics such as economic ethics, moral agency, and the commodification of identity in a globalized world.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of IB 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Christy Newton
IB 673 – Spiritual Sustenance for Social Change
This course explores the spiritual foundations of social change and the practices that sustain it. Students will examine how transformation—personal and institutional—requires deep spiritual work alongside systemic action. Through readings, multimedia resources, discussions, and a writing project, participants will engage spiritual disciplines, reflect critically on their role in justice work, and discover how faith can undergird lasting social transformation.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of IB 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Christy Newton
IB 675 – Ethical Decision Making: Doing the Work Our Souls Must Have
Explore the question, “What is the work your soul must have?” Drawing on womanist theological ethics and personal narratives, this course invites students to discern their inner call toward justice and ethical action. Through spiritual autobiography, storytelling, and critical reflection, participants will synthesize life experiences with theological insights to identify God’s call and develop a framework for purposeful engagement in church, society, and the world.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of IB 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Sharon Ellis Davis
IB 677 - Living Theology in Applachia: The Works of Fr. Rausch
The course will explore the ministry of John Rausch in light of Catholic Social Teaching (CST) with a special focus on the application of CST to Appalachia. The course will have three parts: (1) an exposition of Catholic Social Teaching with a special focus on Pope Francis’ encyclical, Laudato si’; (2) an overview of the history and challenges presented by the economic and environmental context of Appalachia; (3) a survey and analysis of the ministry of John Rausch in light of parts 1 and 2 of the course.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of IB 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
IB 678 - Christian Political Ethics for Social Transformation
This course explores the theological and ethical foundations of Christian socio-political engagement and their implications for social transformation. It introduces students to biblical teachings, theological traditions, moral principles, history, and the writings of major classical as well as contemporary thinkers and how they inform social vision, ethical decisions, and political actions. Through a careful analysis of our contemporary context that addresses pressing issues—including economic inequality, justice, peace, public health, ecological wellbeing, and more—students will have the opportunity to articulate their moral stance, refine their ethical reasoning, and strengthen their political engagement. By the end of the course, students will develop a deeper understanding of how Christian political ethics can shape political engagement, foster social justice, and contribute to the transformation of societies toward greater equity, compassion, human dignity, and shared flourishing.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of IB 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Eleazar Fernandez
IB 679 - Ethics of Hospitality
Migration, exile, and forced displacement are among the defining socio-political and moral crises
of our time. This course examines the ethics of hospitality amid tightening borders, nativist
nationalism, statelessness, and uprooted lives. Students engage philosophical, religious, cultural,
and political perspectives on migration and the structural forces driving displacement and
exclusion. Central themes include justice, belonging, human dignity, solidarity, and
responsibility toward the vulnerable. Through critical readings, dialogue, and case studies,
learners grapple with the tensions between fear and compassion, citizenship and humanity, and
hospitality and hostility, while reflecting on just and humane responses to migration in an
increasingly polarized world.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of IB 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Eleazar Fernandez
IB 680 - God and Nature: Introduction to Environmental Ethics
This class is a survey of the major issues and topics related to environmental ethics and theologies of nature. Beginning with an examination of scriptural and theological dominionism, from there course topics will launch to include animal rights, biocentrism vs. ecocentrism, deep ecology, ecofeminism, climate change, extinction, food ethics, human population, space ethics, wilderness preservation, and environmental disobedience. This course will then focus upon how these issues are engaged within worship, preaching, educational, and missional expressions of the church.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of IB 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Rev. Dr. Chris Rodkey
♦Updated 05/26/26
IF 540 - Contribución Teológica de la Iglesia Latina
Descripción: una exploración de los orígenes, el desarrollo y las principales contribuciones de la teología desarrollada por teólogos y teólogas Latinxs. Se subrayará su importancia y su contribución a la teología en general y a la iglesia en Estados Unidos en particular.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Rev. Dr. Loida I. Martell
IF 541 – Theological Contributions of the Black Church in the US and the World
This course is an examination of the theological innovations that people of African descent have
brought to the Christian faith. We will begin with the period of slavery in America and discuss
the theological evolution of the black church through the 20th century. Our analysis will include
discussion of specific theological symbols and concepts like the cross, sin, redemption,
Christology, theological anthropology, and the bible as a source for theology. We will discuss
these theological symbols and concepts while giving particular attention to race/ethnicity, class,
gender, and analysis of sexuality. We will also discuss Black and Womanist theologies.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
IF 550 – Theology and Theological Language
This course is the prerequisite for all other theology courses. In this course students will be introduced to the basic vocabulary, concepts, paradigms and figures central to studying and practicing theology.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Esther Parajuli
IF 552 – Theology of Sermons
Theology is essential for effective preaching. This is the case because the heart of every sermon is and should be a claim about the nature of God. This theological claim has implications for how we live in community, with ourselves, our congregations, society and Earth itself. In this course, students will learn how to identify theological claims in a sermon and make theological claims from a biblical text that can be used for the purposes of proclamation.

Prerequisite: IF 550 and LW 550
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade & Faculty
IF 553 – Made in the Image of God: Theological Anthropology
Theological anthropology is the study of the human person as created by God. In this module, we will study the central questions with which theologians wrestle when working the theological nature of the human being. We will read and discuss historical and contemporary accounts of sin and what it means to be made in the image of God (Imago Dei). Along the way, we will consider the ethical consequences of particular answers to these questions.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Esther Parajuli
IF 554 – The Nature of God: Theology
In this course we will be considering traditional and contemporary understandings of the nature and work of God. We will look at ideas about creation and providence, God’s dual nature as both immanent and transcendent, theodicy and the nature of God as Trinity.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Esther Parajuli
IF 555 – “One Bread, One Body”: Theology of the Church
In this course we will pay attention to the curious institution that is the church. Most of the time we take church for granted, but when we think about its call, to be both relevant and prophetic, to be grounded in the world with eyes toward the Kingdom of God, it looks not only odd, but maybe impossible. Yet, this is the community Christ called, so we continue to do the best we can in faith that our work will be made right by God. To think about the church, we will study the ways theologians have dealt with difficult questions of how to “be” church and we will apply those theological glimmers to a focused study of our own congregations.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christopher Rodkey
IF 556 – Who Do You Say That I Am: Christology
This course combines two separate but closely related theological doctrines: the study of Christ (his two natures, his works, his death, his place in the Trinity) with a study of salvation, how Christ’s death brings atonement, who is saved and the nature of heaven and hell.

Prerequisite: IF 550 + two additional IF credits
Credit: 1.0 (Offered during On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Dr. Esther Parajuli
IF 557 – Theology and Pastoral Care: Discussing Suffering and Hope
This course explores the theological areas of suffering and evil (theodicy) and visions and practices of hope (eschatology) through the traditions of pastoral theology. Rather than exploring abstract answers that pastors might appeal to for people who are in the midst of crisis, we will explore the ways that communities of faith can be shaped and empowered to understand suffering, to provide communal care, and to pursue visions of hope. We will explore three orders of suffering through an examination of three case studies—considering natural suffering through the challenges of dementia, interpersonal suffering through legacies of trauma, and systemic suffering caused by structures of Neoliberalism. Alongside these orders of suffering, we will consider pastoral practices and visions of hope, especially those of the kingdom of God and the beloved community.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Wilson Dickinson
IF 558 – God Save Us: Soteriology
The doctrine of Soteriology (salvation) integrally depends on the doctrines of Christology, Creation, Theological Anthropology, Theology, Eschatology and Ecclesiology in order to have any meaning all. If you think about it, figuring out what it means to be saved means we have to ask these questions: “From what must we be saved?” By what mechanisms does salvation occur?” and “To what will we be saved?” The theological shortcut for these questions looks like this, “From what/through which/To what?” It is this formula that will guide our time together, as we work together on one of the most difficult questions professional theologians, and lay theologians alike wrestle with which is: “What happened on the cross?”

Prerequisite: IF 550 + two additional IF credits
Credit: 1.0 (Offered during On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Dr. Esther Parajuli
IF 559 – Living the Catholic Experience: Mystery of the Church
This course examines the theological and ethical foundations of creation care within the Catholic tradition and broader Christian contexts. Students will explore eco-spiritual ethics and practices that integrate sustainability into worship, education, and ministry. Through readings, discussions, and practical applications, participants will develop skills to design rituals, programs, and curricula that embody reverence for creation and position the Church as a prophetic witness in addressing climate challenges.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Jean Soto
IF 560 – Living the Catholic Experience: Sacraments I
The Sacraments sit at the center of Roman Catholic life and liturgical practice. Instituted by Jesus Christ and entrusted to the Church, the Sacraments constitute an array of visible signs of an invisible grace by which God draws the Church and its members into God’s life, and empowers God’s people to carry out the Church’s mission in the world. Catholics recognize the existence of seven Sacraments: the Sacraments of Initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, and the Eucharist), the Sacraments of Healing (Reconciliation and the Anointing of the Sick), and the Sacraments of Service (Marriage and Holy Orders). This course treats Catholic sacramentology in general and the Sacraments of Initiation in particular.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
IF 561 – Living the Catholic Experience: Sacraments II
The Sacraments sit at the center of Roman Catholic life and liturgical practice. Instituted by Jesus Christ
and entrusted to the Church, the Sacraments constitute an array of visible signs of an invisible grace by
which God draws the Church and its members into God’s life, and empowers God’s people to carry out
the Church’s mission in the world. Catholics recognize the existence of seven Sacraments: the Sacraments
of Initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, and the Eucharist), the Sacraments of Healing (Reconciliation and
the Anointing of the Sick), and the Sacraments of Service (Marriage and Holy Orders). Building on
“Living the Catholic Experience: Sacraments I,” this course treats the Sacraments of Healing and the
Sacraments of Service.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christopher McMahon

IF 562 – Living the Catholic Experience: Our Sacred Story
This course explores the theological and ethical foundations of creation care within Catholic and broader Christian traditions. Students will examine eco-spiritual ethics and practices that integrate sustainability into worship, education, and ministry. Through readings, discussions, and practical applications, participants will develop skills to design rituals, programs, and curricula that embody reverence for creation and position the Church as a prophetic witness in addressing climate challenges.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Theresa Yugar
IF 563 – Ecclesiologies: From Avatar to Zoom
“Real Presence” is one of the classic questions of Christian theology—often described only as mystery. While this question is historically tied to the practice of the Eucharist, emerging technologies have raised questions about presence, community, and embodiment in digital settings. This course examines theoretical perspectives to this question before returning to practical questions of community and practice as expressed within the contemporary
situation. While wrestling with these matters, we will also develop new skills to apply to digital ministry.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christopher Rodkey
IF 564 – Food Justice and Food Insecurity
This class is a contextual theological exploration of different Christian responses to issues connected with food, especially food insecurity, with the approach of food justice. Students will explore various local and trans-local responses that are informed by justice movements and liberation and decolonial theologies.


Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Wilson Dickinson
IF 565 – Christian Theology and Religious Diversity
In this course we will study the major theological approaches to religious diversity and in doing so, engage with the questions mentioned above. This course will critically examine how the doctrines within Christian theology inform the different approaches to religious diversity. For example, we will consider how a theological understanding of God impact theological approaches to religious diversity, but also how the encounter of religious diversity informs and challenges the Christian understanding of God.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Esther Parajuli
IF 570 – The Church and Homosexuality
This course equips church leaders to engage faithfully and knowledgeably in conversations about sexuality and homosexuality. Students will explore theological, ethical, and pastoral dimensions of these issues to foster dialogue and healing within congregations. Through readings, discussions, and practical resources, participants will gain the understanding necessary to lead communities through divisive topics with compassion, clarity, and integrity.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
IF 572 – Special Topics in Theological Anthropology: Disabilities
In this course we will think about what it means to be made in the image of God through the lens of people with physical, intellectual and developmental disabilities.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
IF 573 – Introduction to the Theology of Paul Tillich
This course is an introduction to the ideas of the Christian philosopher and theologian Paul Tillich. Emphases for this introduction will be focused upon being comfortable with the theological language of Tillich’s writings and contextualizing his ideas into ministerial contexts.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christopher Rodkey
IF 574 – Dietrich Bonhoeffer
This course is an introduction to the ideas of the Christian theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer. Emphases for this introduction will be focused upon Bonhoeffer’s biography, Christology, Ecclesiology, Ethics, and controversial final writings. Students will contextualize these ideas in and for their own ministerial locations and identities.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christopher Rodkey
IF 576 – Contemporary Atheisms
This course is an introduction to the contemporary philosophical and theological issue of disbelief in God. Among subjects to be discussed are classical arguments for and against God; “God” and metaphysical models of the divine; the “New Atheism” movement; radical Christian responses to contemporary atheism; and practical application of these ideas for the purpose of missional leadership and evangelism in the local church.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christopher Rodkey
IF 577 – Narrative Theology
This course introduces students to narrative theology and its significance in Christian thought and practice. Students will explore the narrative quality of human life and Scripture, examine narrative Christology, and consider how narrative shapes identity and political engagement. Through readings and discussions, participants will learn how narrative functions as both a theological lens and a generative mode of expression for faith and ethics.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
IF 578 – Sallie McFague’s Environmental Theology
In this course we will closely consider the origins of theologian Sallie McFague’s environmental work by reading from her groundbreaking work "The Body of God: An Ecological Theology."

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
IF 579 – Reinhold Niebuhr
This course is an introduction to the ideas of the Christian pastor, theologian, and political theorist Reinhold Niebuhr. Students will directly and substantively engage primary texts and learn the political and religious contexts of Reinhold Niebuhr as a major figure of Christian thought whose influence is evident within and beyond the church today. Students in this course will employ Neibuhr’s ideas and style in practical ministerial applications, such as sermons or religious education programs. Finally, course participants will reflect upon the idea of “public theology” within our own contexts of the 21st century.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christopher Rodkey
IF 584 – Food and Faith
This class explores the interaction between contemporary food systems and Christian theology. Food will serve as a lens for seeing these theological traditions in an everyday, incarnational, and contemporary light. We will grapple with issues like hunger, agribusiness, community gardens, global and local economies from the perspective of Christian wisdom. This will allow us to reflect on the role of food in worship, church meals, and service, and as an avenue to help parishioners reflect on their moral lives.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Wilson Dickinson
IF 587 – Theology and Domestic Violence
Think about this: if 1 out of every 3 women in your church and 1 out of every 4 men had cancer, what would the church’s response be? Now think about the fact that these statistics represent the number of women and men who live in relationships characterized by domestic violence, yet the church has been largely silent on this issue.

You will learn how Scripture and theology have been misused to keep people in abusive relationships and how it can be revisioned to help people make difficult decisions about how to deal with abuse. We will ask hard questions about the concepts of covenant, forgiveness, grace and love. You will learn the varieties of ways domestic violence is legally interpreted, beyond getting physically beaten. You will learn about the cycle of abuse that keeps men and women going back into abusive relationships. You will learn about the effects of the opioid epidemic on domestic violence cases and learn to help parents who are being abused by opioid addicted adult children. You will learn how you can help the perpetrators of domestic violence who are also your congregants.


Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
IF 588 – Jesus and Environmental Justice: Christology from Below
This course explores the ways Jesus cultivated grassroots power through renewing convental life, teaching through parables, and transforming communities. We will consider how such efforts might be incarnated in contemporary church and social practice. While both Christology and environmental efforts often begin from above, focusing on cosmic perspectives and hierarchical power, this course will begin from below to consider how the life and ministry of Christ might shape the work of love and justice today.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Wilson Dickinson
IF 589 – Mystical Theology: The Mystery of God and Luminous Life
Mystical Theology names a set of traditions, practices, and ways of life that integrate thinking about God, spiritual formation, and everyday discipleship. This course stages a series of conversations between mystics of the past and contemporary theologians. These dialogues across the centuries will help students think more deeply about the relationships between language, spirituality, and God, and the formative and imaginative poetry of theology and prayer. Along the way we will wrestle with the mystic traditions of darkness and theophany, divine names, love and divine union, the imitation of Christ, and letting go alongside practices of holy reading and contemplation. The mystic path leads us to a clearing where the mystery of God opens the possibility of luminous life.

Prerequisite: IF 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Wilson Dickinson
IF 590 – IF Competency Exercise
*Please refer to section 7.1.6-7.1.8 of the Student Handbook*

Prerequisite: Completion of all other IF 500 level work
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
IF 591 - Theology of Wholeness
This class is an exploration of theological visions of wholeness and social practices that seek to repair communities. This holistic pursuit integrates areas of life that are often compartmentalized from one another—especially the intellectual, the imaginative, the spiritual, the everyday, and the economic. At the heart of our considerations are biblical and theological visions of connection and love—communion, covenant, sabbath, and community. Over the course of this month, our learning community will begin to imagine and engage ways that the frayed threads of our shared world can be woven together into a just and joyful whole.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Wilson Dickinson
IF 592 - Faith and Science Amid Climate Changes
The course will explore climate change through the lens of Christian theology with a special focus on the local experience of LTS students. The course will move along several integrated tracks: (1) an exploration of the theological understanding of Creation and Anthropology from the perspective of Scripture and doctrine; (2) an overview of the challenges presented by climate change science, especially as it affects the context of Appalachia; (3) an assessment of how Christians, their pastors, and congregations can respond in light of tracks 1 and 2 of the course.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Drs. Lisa Graumlich and Christopher McMahon
IF 629 – Understanding Latinx Religion and Spirituality
This course will explore the multiple expressions and varieties of Latino/a/x religion and spirituality, focusing on lived religion. We will explore various understandings of santo and sagrado including rites of passage, worship, and other rituals. These will provide resources for engaging issues of biblical justice, contextual and intersectional identity construction, confronting the evils of racism in the U.S.A, and working toward biblical justice.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and a minimum of 60% of IF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
IF 630 - Beyond Borders: Theology and Religious Pluralism
What should Christians make of religious diversity? This course takes that question seriously, engaging it primarily through the lens of religious pluralism as a theological position. The course will take the theological debate seriously, engaging voices that challenge and voices that embrace religious pluralism, culminating in the contested and lived question of multiple religious belonging.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and a minimum of 60% of IF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Esther S. Parajuli
IF 671 – Gods and Monsters
Religion and horror are inextricable bound. Monsters populate the sacred texts of Judaism and Christianity as well as run rampant in popular culture. In this course we will first consider WHY religion needs monsters. What role do monsters play in religious texts? To help answer this question we will look at Leviathan, Behemoth, Tiamat along with the Whore of Babylon and the beast with the seven heads. Then we will turn our attention to monsters in popular culture. What are the religious aspects of characters like Dracula and Frankenstein? Finally we will consider the complicated history of vampires and Christianity, the rise and fall of the power of the Cross in defeating evil and death.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and a minimum of 60% of IF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
IF 672 – Theology of the Border: US and Mexico
Please join me as we explore what immigration means first hand when we spend seven days on the US/Mexico border at Tucson/Nogales. On this intensive trip you will hear the stories of migration from those who are in the process of crossing or have been deported back, listen to faithful leaders discuss their work with migrants on both sides of the border, walk dirt migrant trails winding through dangerous desert vegetation , experience mass deportation hearings in Federal Court, interview public defenders, dance with migrant children, experience the bitter cold of the desert in winter, sleep on cement floors in migrant shelters, and push yourself emotionally, physically and spiritually in ways you never thought possible. In short you will experience for yourself the complex and painful story of what some refer to as our national wound, the US/Mexico border.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and a minimum of 60% of IF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
IF 673 – Theology and Disabilities
In this course we will work together to think theologically and to read the Bible through the lenses of people with physical, intellectual and developmental disabilities. To do this, we will read first person accounts, contemporary theology, US history and the Bible all with an eye toward becoming a more inclusive and accessible ecclesial community. It is my hope that through your work in this course you are moved to greater activism beyond the church environs and into the community and perhaps the world.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and a minimum of 60% of IF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
IF 674 – Queer Theology
This course explores queer theology as a countercultural, hopeful expression of Christian faith. Students will examine the history and meaning of “queer,” its role in LGBTQIA experiences, and its use in constructive theology to reclaim the disruptive witness of Jesus. Through readings, discussions, and reflection, participants will challenge cultural norms, deepen understanding of identity, and discover how queer insights can inspire fearless, inclusive Christian living.


Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and a minimum of 60% of IF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
IF 675 – Holy Spirit: Beyond Santa and Star Wars
This course seeks to give the student an opportunity to reflect upon the Person of the Spirit as the Third Person of the Trinity. Who is the Spirit? What is the relation of the Spirit to the Parent and to the Christ? What is the role of the Spirit in soteriology and eschatology? Is the role of the Spirit only confined to the ecclesiology or does God the Spirit have a greater global presence than the Western Church has heretofore granted the Spirit? Emphasis will be made on the role of the Spirit as Life-giver and its implications for contemporary contexts.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and a minimum of 60% of IF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Loida Martell
IF 677 – Postcolonial Theology
The impact of European colonialism, which began in the 15th century, on our understanding of difference across political, economic, social, cultural, and religious dimensions is indisputable. This course aims to subject this colonial construction of difference and sameness to theological inquiry by delving into postcolonial theory and theology.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and a minimum of 60% of IF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Esther Parajuli
IF 681 – Theology and Emerging Science
In an increasingly technocratic world, one which faces the dangers of emergent viral diseases such as COVID-19, avian flu virus, and the perplexity of artificial intelligence encroaching in our everyday lives, how do pastors respond to the ethical, moral, biblical, and theological questions that arise among their congregations? This course is designed to explore some of the scientific challenges that face people of faith that include climate change, artificial intelligence, science denialism, popular pseudosciences, post-pandemic vaccinations (and their denial on various grounds), and other related issues, all within the context of how these issues impact culture, politics, and engaged communities of belief.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and a minimum of 60% of IF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Chris Rodkey
IF 682 - Nation and Belonging: Feminist Political Theologies in a Fractured World
This course engages feminist political theology to examine the contested constructions of nation, citizenship, and belonging. Attending to the ways religious language, symbols, and practices sacralize and secure national identities, we will explore how feminist theologians interrogate and disrupt these formations. The course centers theological traditions that reimagine the body politic and the divine as generative spaces of kinship, refusal, and radical belonging. Through these engagements, students will consider the pastoral, ethical, and liturgical possibilities for nurturing communities that exist beyond the logics of the nation-state.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and a minimum of 60% of IF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Esther Parajuli
♦ Updated 03/30/26
IP 540 - Historia De la Iglesia Latinx
Esta clase se dedica a contar la historia de los latinxs en la historia del cristianismo en el continente americano. Exploraremos las diversas maneras en que llegó el cristianismo desde el período colonial hasta el presente, enfocándonos en el impacto actual que los cristianos latinxs están teniendo en la vida social, política y religiosa en la región. Esta clase analizara la larga historia desde el período de colonización hasta el presente. Los estudiantes aprenderán sobre momentos, personas, y eventos claves en la historia de la Iglesia en América del Norte y el importante papel que los latinxs han tenido en la configuración de la vida religiosa y social.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Stephen R. DiTrolio
IP 541 - CHurch HIstory through African American Eyes
This course explores the history of African American Christianity through the eyes and experiences of Black people in the United States. It examines the origins of slave religion in colonial period through the development of the Black Church through the civil rights era and beyond. Ultimately, this course provides an opportunity to develop a theological imagination that considers the spiritual narratives and experiences as told from the perspectives of African Americans.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Edward J. Robinson
IP 550 – Early and Medieval Church History: A Global Perspective
When Christianity appeared on the world stage it entered an environment of diverse cultures that shaped multiple religious identities, beliefs, and practices. This four-week intensive will examine Christianity as a global/world religious movement during the 1st through 14th centuries in the Eastern and Western Churches. It will trace the spread of Christianity throughout the Greco-Roman world and beyond and it will explore some of the distinctive expression of and responses to Christianity in these contexts. It will also provide space for dialogue about the impact of this dynamic religious history on contemporary ministry today.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Douglas Clark
IP 551 – Reformation to Contemporary Church History: A Global Perspective
This course is a general overview of the history of Christianity from the end of the Protestant Reformation to the early twentieth century.

This course includes a required assignment in your current congregation to lead/teach a lesson/discussion on a particular element/event of/in church history. This can take place in Sunday School, a small group setting, or before the whole congregation (not appropriate for Sunday morning worship). You should begin to make arrangements for this as soon as you have registered for the course. If you are unable to schedule this assignment in your congregation, you must ask the instructor before the course begins for an alternate assignment to satisfy the course requirement.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0 (Offered during On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Dr. Douglas Clark
IP 552 – Living the Catholic Experience: Tradition I
This course introduces the Catholic tradition, tracing its development from the early church to the Catholic Reformation. Students will explore how faith is transmitted through texts, doctrines, and practices, and engage key figures such as Augustine, Aquinas, Teresa of Ávila, and John of the Cross. Through readings and discussions, participants will discover the richness of Catholic tradition and its diverse expressions of God’s self-revelation in Jesus Christ.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christopher McMahon
IP 553 – Living the Catholic Experience: Tradition II
This course will study the documents of Vatican II as they relate to the new face of the Catholic Church post Vatican II. The spirit and theology in the Documents of Vatican II will be studied and the changes to the Church will be evaluated and contrasted with the pre-Vatican II Roman Catholic Church. The impact of Vatican II on ecumenism, and cultural openness to the world (aggiornamento) will be reviewed. An initial exploration of the rise of liberation theologies in conjunction with the new call to aggiornamento generated by Vatican II will be undertaken.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christopher McMahon
IP 570 – Disciples History & Polity I
This course is an overview of the history and polity of the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ) from its beginnings on the American frontier to the present day.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Rev. Dr. Lon Oliver and Rev. Dr. Don Gillett, II
IP 572 – The Religious Awakening of America
This course is a brief overview of the Great Awakening, which occurred in the American colonies in the early and mid-eighteenth century. The course is a survey of the political, cultural, and social consequences of the Awakening.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
IP 573 – The Second Great Awakening
This course is a brief overview of the Great Awakening, which occurred in the American colonies in the early and mid- eighteenth century. The course is a survey of the political, cultural, and social consequences of the Awakening.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
IP 576 – Religion in the Civil Rights Movement
This course is a brief overview of the American Civil Rights Movement of the 1950s and 1960s. It will focus on the experiences of those in leadership who self-identified as Christians. We will use their lives as examples of how our ministry today can shape and mold the lives of our parishioners and our congregations.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Douglas Clark
IP 577 – The Church and Race Relations in America
This course is a very basic overview of the role Christianity played in the Civil Rights Movement of the 1950s and 1960s.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
IP 581 – UCC History and Polity I
This is an online course on the History, Polity, and Theology of the United Church of Christ (UCC) based on the Marks of Faithful and Effective Authorized Ministers (The Marks). It is structured in community with other students. It may fulfill portions of the “Essential Elements” guideline developed by the UCC History & Polity Teachers’ Network. Through readings, multi-media presentations, discussion forums, and a writing project, we will engage in community dialogue and written reflection to understand the history, polity, and ecclesiology of the United Church of Christ.

This course may satisfy a requirement of UCC Committees on Ministry for authorization as ordained or lay ministers in the Indiana Kentucky Conference of the United Church of Christ. It may also fulfill the requirements for Authorized Ministry in other UCC Associations and Conferences, if approved. In addition, it provides an introduction for ministers from other denominations seeking privilege of call, ministerial partnership standing or dual standing in the UCC.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
IP 582 – Augustine
This course introduces Augustine’s theology and its lasting influence on Christian thought. Students will explore his theological method, engagement with Neoplatonism, views on grace and human will during the Pelagian controversy, and homilies on love and community. Through readings, lectures, and discussions, participants will critically assess Augustine’s contributions to doctrines of God, humanity, church, and ethics, and consider their relevance for contemporary ministry and theological reflection.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
IP 584 – American Religious Diversity
This two-week, half-credit course introduces the rich diversity of religious traditions in U.S. history. Students will explore the role of immigration in shaping Protestant, Catholic, Jewish, and African American religious expressions, including Christianity, Islam, and conjuring traditions. The course also examines unique practices such as serpent-handling in Appalachia. Through readings and discussions, participants will develop skills for engaging across religious differences as pastoral leaders.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Douglas Clark
IP 587 – Women, Religious Narratives, and U.S. History
This course invites students to explore the various ways that women have been depicted in religious narrative during the 18th and 19th centuries in the US. It will examine the contributions of women as well as the discourses that shaped them. Students will be challenged to reflect on their own assumptions, perspectives and attitudes about women and religion and discuss the implications for contemporary ministry.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Julia Speller
IP 588 – Christians and Material Wealth in Gregory and Francis
This course examines Christian perspectives on wealth and power through the lives and teachings of Gregory the Great and St. Francis of Assisi. Students will explore how churches navigate material resources and authority, and how followers of Jesus discern personal stewardship. Through readings and discussions, participants will critically reflect on ethical questions of giving, keeping, and leading faithfully in a world where wealth and power intersect.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Donald Brash
IP 590 – IP Competency Exercise
*Please refer to section 7.1.6-7.1.8 of the Student Handbook*

Prerequisite: Completion of all other IP 500 level work
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Douglas Clark
IP 591 - Early Christian Women
This course explores the roles of women in early Christianity (2nd–4th centuries CE), focusing on leadership, martyrdom, and pilgrimage. It examines how gender, sexuality, and celibacy shaped women’s contributions to theology and church institutions, often in tension with Roman norms. Students will study the diversity of women’s participation and reflect on how this history informs contemporary pastoral leadership, especially for women and gender/sexual minority groups in ministry.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Douglas Brown Clark
IP 592 - Revival and Reform in the 19th Century United States
This course provides an introduction to the history of revivalism in the 19th century United States, focusing on the movement known as the Second Great Awakening. It examines the origins, distinctive features, and legacies of this series of revivals. It assesses the rise in popularity of Arminian theologies, the importance of frontier contexts, and the dramatic numerical rise of Methodists and Baptists, and the creation of new movements and denominations such as the Stone-Campbell Movement and Mormonism / Latter-Day Saints. The course focuses in with particular attention to the connections between these revivals and social, racial, and gender justice and inclusion, in particular through the involvement of African Americans, including the abolitionist activism of Christians like Frederick Douglass and Angelina Grimké, as well as the major revolts against slavery which were inspired by revivals, led by Nat Turner and Denmark Vesey. The course seeks to assist students in drawing on revival-related theologies and connecting those theologies to social justice as they develop their own capacities as pastoral leaders to encourage others in the pursuit of a deep faith an authentic, socially responsible life.
IP 670 – Disciples History & Polity II
This course explores the theological and cultural roots of the Stone-Campbell Movement and its 200-year history. Students will examine key reformers, historical contexts, and the movement’s impact on congregational life and mission today. Through readings and discussions, participants will assess the relevance of its theology and missiology for contemporary ministry and conclude with an analysis of the current polity and structure of the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ).

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and 60% of 500 level IP work
Credit: 2.0 (Offer during On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Rev. Dr. Lon Oliver
IP 673 – UCC Polity, History, & Theology
This is a course in the History, Polity, and Theology of the United Church of Christ (UCC). It is designed to satisfy academic requirements in UCC History and Polity for lay and ordained persons preparing for authorized ministry in the UCC. Through readings, videos, multi-media presentations, discussion forums, and a writing project, we will engage in community dialogue and written reflection to understand the history, polity, and ecclesiology of the United Church of Christ. This course fulfills a requirement of UCC Committees on Ministry for authorization as ordained or lay ministers in the Indiana Kentucky Conference of the United Church of Christ. It may also fulfill the requirements for Authorized Ministry in other UCC Associations and Conferences, if approved. In addition, it provides an introduction for ministers from other denominations seeking privilege of call or ministerial standing in the UCC.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and 60% of 500 level IP work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
IP 676/876 Formative Transitions in the Early Churches
Contemporary discussions around differences among Christians often refer to the early churches. The churches of the first 600 years established foundations with which we continue to be in dialogue. The often-stated idea is that what was most original is the most authoritative. Close examination demonstrates that the ideas, practices, and organizational structures from this period of the development of Christianity are varied, complex, and sometimes conflicted. This course will look at key players and pivotal moments of the patristic legacy to better discern their contemporary value.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and 60% of 500 level IP work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
IP 677/877 - Vanished Churches: Christianity in the East
This course explores the rich and often overlooked history of Eastern Christianity, from its early flourishing to its gradual decline. Students will examine the theological, cultural, and political development of churches such as the Nestorian, Syriac, Coptic, and Armenian traditions, and their significant roles in the broader Christian and Islamic worlds. The course traces the golden ages of these communities—marked by scholarship, missionary work, and interreligious dialogue—as well as the pressures of empire, persecution, and shifting demographics that led to their marginalization as a largely forgotten chapter of global Christianity.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one Competency Exercise and 60% of 500 level IP work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Jon Barnes
♦ Updated 03/30/26
IS 520 – The Origin, Inspiration, and Authority of the Church’s Scripture
The purpose of this class is to introduce you to some of the issues that influence how we understand and use the Bible. We will explore how books became important for the faith community of the Israelites, how the Bible came together as a book, and what it means to say that the Bible is inspired. We will also explore ways to appropriate the biblical text for today so that it can be a guide for the church’s beliefs and practices. The goal of this study is to prepare you to do more detailed study of the texts and to use them in your ministry. This course intends to help you begin to understand these texts so that you may use them in legitimate and meaningful ways in your congregations and so that you and they may hear the word of God and be given a basis for faithful living.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 521 - African American Biblical Hermeneutics
This course takes up the intersection between politics and biblical interpretation. It turns to specific Hebrew Bible and
New Testament texts to think with students about the purposes and work of AABI. The course addresses ways that these
texts have been used traditionally and, as liberative praxis, the course will work through ways of re-reading texts as
resistance. As praxis, this course works with students to develop their own hermeneutical understandings as a self-
reflective exercise and their facility to engage difficult biblical texts and challenge interpretive practices of
marginalization.

Prerequisite: none
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Nauff Zakaria
IS 522 – Leyendo la Biblia a través de Lentes Hispanos
Leyendo la Biblia a Través de Lentes Hispanos es un curso asincrónico en línea de una hora de crédito que introduce al estudiante a los elementos sociohistóricos, teológicos, literarios e interpretativos de la Biblia en cinco módulos de estudio. Impulsado por conferencias, discusiones en clase, tareas interactivas y recursos diversos, este estudio del texto bíblico está diseñado para acompañar a los estudiantes en un enfoque creativo y contextual de la Biblia desde la mirada de los grupos hispanos para facilitar la interpretación de la presencia de Dios en el mundo que habitamos.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Doris J. Garcia Rivera
IS 523 - Las Comadres: El Exegesis del Libro de Rút como el Acompañamiento Bíblico
En este curso, el instructor y los estudiantes abordarán la exégesis bíblica desde un marco teológico del acompañamiento bíblico. El acompañamiento bíblico se refiere a las formas en que el texto bíblico ha servido a las comunidades de fe como palabra y presencia de Dios en sus jornadas de fe, en la experiencia humana, y en sus expresiones de cultura e identidad. Utilizarán el Libro de Rut como caso práctico de este método inductivo y relacional de interpretación bíblica. El objetivo de este curso es ayudar a integrar los enfoques exegéticos de los estudios bíblicos con la formación espiritual e interseccional del exegeta.
Prerequisite: IS 522
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Sophia Magallanes-Tsang
IS 525 - Jesus, Love, and Non-Violent Resistance
In this course, students explore how the gospel of Jesus Christ can be understood as good news in our contemporary world. Specifically, students will discover that the gospel is good news because it resists authoritarian political power with the power of love. However, biblical interpreters often overlook this significance because they misunderstand the context of the gospel and the ministry of Jesus. Therefore, in this course, students will be invited to investigate the ways the gospel of Jesus resists imperialism, violence, and authoritarian politics. Students will examine the imperial and authoritarian context of the first century, engage interpretations of Jesus that emphasize liberation, nonviolence, and social transformation, and consider the ongoing significance of the ministry of Jesus in today’s context. Ultimately, students are equipped to understand the good news in the ancient context and apply its significance in contemporary social and political contexts. 

Prerequisite: IS 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Rev. Dr. Dain Smith
IS 540 – Reading the Torah in the Church Today
This course is a narrative exegetical approach to the pentateuchal books of the Torah (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy) for the Christian faith. The primary point of the course is not for the professor to expound an interpretation or interpretations of these books of the Torah, but for you to learn and practice critical exegetical skills for understanding and elucidating narrative texts within these books of Torah for your own edification and the edification of congregants. You will engage and practice exegetical skills, including those related to narrative criticism, source criticism, and form criticism that will aid you in drawing out meaning (exegeting) narratives in the pentateuchal books of the Torah

Prerequisite: IS 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Doris Garcia-Rivera
IS 541 – Reading the Prophets in the Church Today
This course provides a broad overview of the prophetic books of the Hebrew Bible, with a particular focus on the book of Isaiah. The course examines literary genres or forms that appear in prophetic texts; sets these books in their ancient social, economic, political, literary, and religious contexts; and asks how their messages are relevant to the life and witness of the church today.

Prerequisite: IS 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. John Hull
IS 542 – Reading the Deuteronomistic History in the Church Today
This course surveys Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings—texts known as the Historical Books or Former Prophets, collectively called the Deuteronomistic History. Students will explore Israel’s rise and fall in the land, from conquest to exile, and examine key figures such as Joshua, Deborah, David, and Solomon. Through readings and discussions, participants will learn how these narratives frame the Hebrew Bible and serve as foundational stories for the New Testament.

Prerequisite: IS 520
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. John Hull
IS 543 – The Bible, Creation, and Justice
This course examines the intersection of the Bible, ecology, and justice through ecowomanist frameworks. Students will analyze creation narratives, theological models of stewardship and domination, and the links between environmental crises and social hierarchies of race, class, and gender. Through readings, discussions, and writing, participants will uncover ecological wisdom in Scripture and ecowomanist thought, developing theological responses and strategies for earth-care and social justice that affirm all members of creation.

Prerequisite: IS 520
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
IS 544 – Reading the Bible from the Margins
This course introduces historical criticism and its role in biblical interpretation while exploring alternative approaches that have emerged over the past fifty years. Students will examine narrative criticism, liberation theology, feminist readings, and other perspectives that challenge traditional Euro-American scholarship. Through readings and discussions, participants will learn how diverse voices and social contexts shape interpretation, developing skills for engaging Scripture critically and inclusively.

Prerequisite: IS 520
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. John Hull
IS 545 – Church and Social Issues: What the Bible Says
This course will survey the ways religion and the Bible have been used in the United States to discuss social issues. We will also discuss a consistent way to use Biblical texts to inform the positions we take and advocate on Social Issues. We will then turn to specific issues that have been controversial, looking at how the Biblical text can address them faithfully. The purpose of this study is to enable you to engage the church in these matters so that it works to move the world closer to what God would have it be. We will see how Scripture calls the church to work for justice and mercy in our social systems.

Prerequisite: IS 520
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 553 – Preparing to Help the Church Read the New Testament for Today
This course introduces the political and religious context of the New Testament to prepare students for deeper study of its texts. Students will explore the life circumstances of Jesus and the early church, learning to interpret Scripture within its historical setting. Through readings and discussions, participants will develop skills for faithful, informed use of the New Testament in ministry and cultivate disciplined listening for God’s voice through study.

Prerequisite: IS 520
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 554 – The Gospels as Resources for the Church
This course will examine the Gospels carefully. The course enables students to discern what kinds of writings are found in the Gospels and what we should expect to find in them. Reflection upon how the Gospels are related to one another and how they are used in recent discussions of the historical Jesus will be included. The course will also examine each Gospel in some detail, looking for what the writer of each wanted readers to think about Jesus, God, and the world. This will help us think about what they say to the church today.

Prerequisite: IS 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 556 – Pauline Letters as Resources for the Church
This course will set each Pauline letter in its original setting, noticing how each is a pastoral and theological response to the social, spiritual, and theological questions and problems that had arisen in the church to which he writes. It will examine how he interprets the gospels in ways that address that church’s concerns and shows them how to be faithful to God and the gospel in the pluralistic society of the first century. The course also explores ways to appropriate these texts for the church today, as we think about how our spiritual and religious concerns have some analogies with theirs, and how Paul’s responses to these questions do and do not give us guidance in today’s church.

Prerequisite: IS 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 560 – Exegesis for the Church
This course will teach the techniques of historical-critical exegesis. We will look at the methods that help readers of the Bible come to understand what the text meant in its original setting. It also explores the way that these results can be appropriated for the church today so that the Bible can help lead the churches beliefs and practices.

Prerequisite: 3 Hours of Required IS Credits
Credit: 2.0 (Offered During On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 573 – Ruth and Jonah
This course offers an in-depth study of the short narratives of Ruth and Jonah, two unique four-chapter books in the Hebrew Bible. Though set in Israel’s past, these stories likely address later issues and take unconventional approaches to traditional themes. Ruth explores loyalty and identity through an unexpected alliance between a Judean and a Moabite, while Jonah—unlike any other prophetic book—examines God’s mercy and justice. Students will engage these texts critically, discovering fresh interpretive insights and practical applications for teaching and preaching in contemporary congregations.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. John Hull
IS 574 – Paul and Women
This course will explore what Paul and those who wrote in his name said about women in leadership roles in the church. We will also give attention to how one appropriates Scripture for the church today.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 575 – The Book of Amos
This course focuses on exegesis of the Book of Amos. Amos is considered the earliest of the so-called “writing prophets” or, perhaps better, the earliest prophetic book. The opening sentence indicates Amos addresses Israel in the eighth century BCE. Subsequent prophetic books predict disaster for Israel and Judah as the Mesopotamian powers encroach. However, Amos, writing in a period of relative prosperity announced the End of Israel. The course will emphasize learning exegetical skills as well as discovering the message of Amos.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. John Hull
IS 578 – Ezra-Nehemiah
This course offers a literary and theological exploration of Ezra-Nehemiah, examining its role as a narrative of Judah’s restoration during the Persian period. Students will analyze the text’s literary strategies and socio-historical context, considering how this pivotal era shaped the religious experiences that influenced both the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament. Through close reading and discussion, the course invites reflection on Ezra-Nehemiah’s theological significance and its relevance for Christian faith today, fostering insights for pastoral application and contemporary interpretation.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
IS 580 – Reading the Hebrew Bible During Advent
This course emphasizes three areas. First, it examines a selection of texts from the Hebrew Bible that are read during Advent. Second, it leads students in reading critically the familiar Nativity Stories in the Gospels. In the reading we pay particular attention to the way these texts make use of the Hebrew Bible. Students learn to investigate historical context and theological meaning. Third, the course helps students think about what it means to be readers of biblical texts and helps them read these texts from new perspectives.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. John Hull
IS 581 – Reading the Hebrew Bible in the Broader Religious and Civic Community
This course explores the use of the Hebrew Bible in the public square as a source for ethical and political dialogue. The first half examines the Bible as a political document, tracing its diverse views on governance, justice, and the public dimensions of faith. Students will then engage contemporary issues, including the First Amendment’s “wall of separation” and key Supreme Court rulings shaping religion and government in America. The course concludes with an introduction to Scriptural Reasoning, an interfaith movement fostering dialogue among Jews, Christians, Muslims, and others to promote justice, peace, and shared understanding.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
IS 582 – Reading the Gospels in Advent
This course discusses the meaning of Advent and the meaning of Lectionary texts for the particular year in which the course is taught. It gives attention to the meaning of these texts in their settings within the Gospels and their meanings as texts read within the season of Advent.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 583 – Reading the Bible in Lent
This course discusses the meaning of Lent and the meaning of the Lectionary texts for the particular year in which the course is taught. It gives attention to the meaning of these texts in their literary and historical settings and their meanings as texts read within the season of Lent.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 584-1 – Reading Colossians
This course will explore the Letter to the Colossians. In addition to examining its historical setting and literary forms, we will see what it continues to say to the church. We will look at its affirmations about Christ and the church and at its demands for the Christian life. We will see a church struggling to understand and live out the faith in a pluralistic and non-Christian world.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 585 – Revelation
This course will begin a study of the Book of Revelation. It will do so by introducing the literary form and theological outlook of Apocalyptic. Only after we understand this movement and its literature will we be able to read Revelation with clarity. We will look at the matters of a Critical Introduction for Revelation. We will work through the text of this fascinating book, exploring how its message can speak to the church and world today.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 587 – Black Queer Hermeneutics: Reading Galatians with Baldwin and Lorde
This course will begin a study of the Book of Revelation. It will do so by introducing the literary form and theological outlook of Apocalyptic. Only after we understand this movement and its literature will we be able to read Revelation with clarity. We will look at the matters of a Critical Introduction for Revelation. We will work through the text of this fascinating book, exploring how its message can speak to the church and world today.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Eric Thomas
