IS 589 - Philippians
This course provides an in-depth study of Philippians, focusing on its critical and theological themes beyond what is covered in the general Epistles course. Topics include Christology, friendship, financial ethics, imitation, and Christian community. Through disciplined reading and reflection, students will learn to interpret Philippians for preaching and teaching, hearing God’s voice in the text and applying its insights for faithful living. Emphasizing the Bible as central to Christian leadership, this course nurtures both scholarly understanding and spiritual formation as essential practices for ministry.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 590 – IS Competency Exercise
*Please refer to section 7.1.6-7.1.8 of the Student Handbook*

Prerequisite: Completed All 500-level IS Required Coursework
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 592 - Reading the Bible Amid Climate Challenges
This course explores the Bible as a resource for engaging in conversations about climate change. Students will examine biblical texts and themes including creation, punishment, and ecological care, and analyze how these ancient texts relate to contemporary discourse on this topic. With attention to the Torah, prophetic and wisdom literature, weekly discussions will center on the role of God and humans in the care of the Earth.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Samaria Divine
IS 593 - Decolonizing the New Testament
Decolonizing how we read Scripture is important because we all live in a world conditioned by imperialism and colonialism. Moreover, the Bible has often been weaponized and used to legitimize imperial expansion, colonial violence, enslavement, harm, division, and oppression. Therefore, it is important for biblical interpreters and religious leaders to untangle the New Testament from these problematic realities and produce healthier theologies. This course introduces students to postcolonial criticism in New Testament (NT) studies in order to equip students with theoretical frameworks that investigate the problematic ways imperialism and colonialism affect, and has affected, New Testament interpretation, theology, and religious practice. Ultimately, this course equips students to reconstruct NT interpretations and theologies that liberate instead of dominate, cultivate instead of manipulate, and redeem instead of demean.

Prerequisite: IS 520 and IS 560
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Rev. Dr. Dain Smith
IS 625 – The Bible and Public Policy
This course will discuss what we find in the Bible about the relationship between our faith and political institutions and discourse. We will look at the ways the Bible addresses social, economic, and political issues in the contexts in which the people lived and the texts were written. We will also look at the ways the Bible has been used, particularly in the U.S. to address this kinds of issues. The purpose of this study is to enable you to engage the church in these matters so that it works to move the world closer to what God would have it be.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of a competency exercise and 60% of the IS 500-level work.
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 630 - Freedom, Evil, and Biblical Interpretation
This course takes up the intersection between politics and biblical interpretation. It turns to specific Hebrew Bible and New Testament texts to interrogate particular manifestations of evil in the contemporary world. The course addresses ways that these texts have been used to affirm certain evils and, as liberative praxis, the course will work through ways of re-reading text in order to subvert evil. As praxis, this course works with students to develop their own hermeneutical understandings as a self-reflective exercise and their facility to engage difficult biblical texts and challenge `interpretive practices of marginalization.

Prerequsite: Successful completion of a competency exercise and 60% of the IS 500-level work
Faculty
Credits: 2.0
IS 672 – The Gospel of Mark
This course will engage in a detailed study of the Gospel of Mark. We will examine the text in its historical context, but also note the ways Mark creates a narrative through which he wants the readers to come to a proper understanding of Jesus and of life in the Kingdom of God. We will further look for ways this text speaks to the church today. The course will require students to continue to hone their skills in using Scripture in the church.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of a competency exercise and 60% of the IS 500-level work.
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 675 – Pauline Sites in Greece & Turkey
TBA

Prerequisite: Successful completion of a competency exercise and 60% of the IS 500-level work.
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 678 – Romans
This course will be an in depth study of Paul’s letter to the Romans. We will work to see how his argument works, what theological assertions he makes and how he uses them. We will also think about how what Paul says to the Romans should speak to the church today.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of a competency exercise and 60% of the IS 500-level work.
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Jerry Sumney
IS 679 – African American Biblical Interpretation for the Church Life
This course takes up the intersection between politics and biblical interpretation in and among African American ecclesial communities. It attends to the ways these communities have deployed the texts, themes, symbols, and idiom of the Bible toward liberative praxis. Its emphasis focuses on the textuality of texts (that is, both the life world and African American interpretive work)—as mediated by biblical interpretation. As praxis, this course works with students to develop their own hermeneutical understandings as a self-reflective exercise and their facility to engage difficult biblical texts, which have traditionally been used and interpretive practices of marginalization.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of a competency exercise and 60% of the IS 500-level work.
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Herbert Marbury
IS 680/880 - A Liberation Biblical Hermeneutics for Lent
This course reimagines Lent as a season for liberative interpretation and preaching. Engaging the socio-political world of Roman Judea, students will examine how the passion narratives may have been shaped by imperial interests and explore strategies for recovering their anti-imperial message. Through hermeneutical reflection and praxis, the course equips students to engage difficult biblical texts critically, challenge marginalizing interpretations, and develop their own liberative approaches for preaching and teaching. Emphasizing theological depth and social awareness, this course fosters interpretive practices that connect faith with justice and transformation.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of a competency exercise and 60% of the IS 500-level work.
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Herbert Marbury
♦ Updated 03/30/26
LC 520 – Pastoral Care Modalities
The course introduces students to basic assumptions, practices, and theological reflections of pastoral care, with special emphasis on individual encounters between a care-giver and care receiver. The class will also ask students to explore pastoral care experiences in their own lives and the ways their personal history, identity, and context impact their understanding of care.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Beth Toler
LC 540 - Cuidado Pastoral en el Contexto Latinx
Este curso está diseñado para profundizar en las ideologías que informan nuestro cuidado pastoral, identificar
desafíos culturales del contexto latinx, y entender las herramientas necesarias para proveer un cuidado pastoral
digno y eficaz. El curso es asincrónico en línea de una hora de crédito donde tomaremos el tiempo de explorar
motivación individual y teológica de lo que entendemos como cuidado pastoral -incluyendo definiciones de
sufrimiento, acompañamiento, sanidad integral, etcétera e identificaremos herramientas necesarias y eficaces en
estos tiempos complejos y contextos ministeriales. El curso será formado de conferencias, tareas interactivas,
discusiones de clase y recursos diversos que formarán un conocimiento práctico para acompañar sus labores
ministeriales.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Rev. Alexandra Zareth
LC 541 - Pastoral Care in the African American Context
In the African American context, the tradition of storytelling has not only enabled the dissemination and preservation of African and African American culture, but it has also provided spiritual and emotional care during hardships while encouraging a sense of community. With the practice of pastoral care being continually informed and influenced by the need to develop creative ways to respond to the contextual needs and challenges of others, this course will explore a narrative/storytelling approach to pastoral care as a means of responding to the contextual needs and challenges in the African American church, while providing students with practical knowledge in implementing storytelling, story listening, and counter-storytelling in caring for others.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Michael Palmer
LC 550 – Creating a Congregational Culture of Care
Creating a Congregational Culture of Care During this course, we will seek together to develop your role as a pastoral caregiver within the congregational context and to cultivate your gifts in equipping the entire congregation to be a community of care. To achieve this, we’ll investigate theories, methods and practices of pastoral care and counseling, and will explore the role of theological reflection within the contexts of congregational care. We will consider how our embedded and operative theologies impact our approach and role in care giving. We will also engage a diverse selection of scholars in theology, systems theory and organizational dynamics. All these areas will be examined through the varying lenses of gender, cultural, national, racial, ethnic, ability, class and sexual difference.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Beth Toler
LC 552 – Diagnosis & Referral: Lost Art of Listening
This course is designed to introduce students to skills for effective pastoral care giving. Students will learn the art of pastoral listening through instruction, practice and feedback, thus helping to improve interpersonal self-awareness. This course introduces the topics of pastoral assessment/diagnosis and intervention, with specific attention to learning when and how to refer a person to additional sources of care.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Francesca Nuzzolese
LC 554 – The Art of Visitation
Visitation is one of many activities which fall under the larger heading of pastoral care. As such, this course builds on theories and practices covered in LC 520 Pastoral Care Modalities with the intent of aiding the student in becoming a more self-aware and effective pastoral care giver.

This course will not recommend any one method for visitation, but will facilitate reflection on the various advantages and disadvantages of different options for doing visits and implementing a visitation program. It will argue for and try to facilitate deep awareness of even the small decisions and moments in this incarnational ministry. The nature and work of God. We will look at ideas about creation and providence, God’s dual nature as both immanent and transcendent, theodicy and the nature of God as Trinity.

This course includes a required assignment in your current congregation to conduct and reflect on a congregational visit. You should begin to make arrangements for this as soon as you have registered for the course. If you are unable to schedule this assignment in your congregation, you must ask the instructor before the course begins for an alternate assignment to satisfy the course requirement.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Beth Toler
LC 556 - Understanding and Engaging Religious and Spiritual Struggles
Major life crises can affect people not only psychologically, socially, and physically but spiritually as well by raising profoundly unsettling questions: How can God allow such pain and suffering? Am I being punished? Do I still believe in God? How can I live up to my spiritual values? Has my religious community abandoned me? Does my life have a deeper ultimate purpose and meaning?

In the last 25 years, these kinds of religious/spiritual struggles have begun to receive attention from medical and mental health researchers and practitioners. This growing body of work not only validates that religious/spiritual struggles are an important part of the human experience, it also has revealed significant correlations and implications for physical and mental health and well-being. This course will highlight this new research, invite students to identify spiritual struggles commonly encountered in the context of chaplaincy and ministry, and explore strategies of care for addressing religious/spiritual struggles.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Beth Toler
LC 571 – Loss & Grief in a Community of Faith
At times of death, dying and bereavement, human limitations are attested. Pastoral care givers have a powerful opportunity to minister to persons and communities in such times. By exploring death and dying process students will have an opportunity to bring such reality closer to themselves. By looking into grief theories, students will develop pastoral care giving skills to utilize in such times. Such exploration will be brought to the context of church ministry especially to the context of funeral to conclude this course.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
LC 574 – Trauma & Recovery
This course aims to foster students’ capacity to reflect on and respond to traumatic injuries and trauma survivors as pastoral care provider. The historical background of such reflection will be studied through the reading material and various practical issues that a religious responder needs to know about in caring for trauma survivors will be examined and practiced. Based on such knowledge students will foster pastoral sensitivity through theological reflections on experiences of trauma.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
LC 576 – Pastoral Care and Substance Abuse
The course introduces students to basic assumptions, practices, and theological reflections of pastoral care and substance abuse, with special emphasis on the alcoholics anonymous model.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Richard Coble
LC 579 – Models of Faith Development and Spiritual Growth
This course explores spiritual growth as an intentional process shaped by faith, contrasting it with biological and emotional development. Drawing on James Fowler’s research on stages of faith and insights from mystics and contemporary spiritual writers, students will examine theoretical frameworks and practical tools for guiding individuals and communities toward spiritual maturity. Using a pastoral theological approach, the course emphasizes assessment, reflective practice, and strategies for fostering growth. Students will engage in experiential learning to develop skills for accompanying others on their spiritual journey and addressing one of the most urgent needs of our time: spiritual depth.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Francesca Nuzzolese
LC 580 – Power, Privilege, & Difference
How do we take power and privilege into account when we provide pastoral care? This question can be approached from many different angles. In this course, we will explore this question by examining different layers of relationship in which power dynamics happen: we will consider power, privilege and differences in the context of professional ethics, family system thinking and the challenges of multiculturality and hybridity. This course requires the students to engage in serious self-reflection to see the self in the various power dynamic contexts by utilizing the course material proactively.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Richard Coble
LC 581 – Care of Persons, Care of Worlds: Social Justice and Care
How do we take power and privilege into account when we provide pastoral care? This question can be approached from many different angles. In this course, we will explore this question by examining different layers of relationship in which power dynamics happen: we will consider power, privilege and differences in the context of professional ethics, family system thinking and the challenges of multiculturality and hybridity. This course requires the students to engage in serious self-reflection to see the self in the various power dynamic contexts by utilizing the course material proactively.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Richard Coble
LC 582 – Climate Change: Caring for Our Planet, Caring for Ourselves
What is the connection between our mental and spiritual health and the health of the planet? How might our commitments to the earth enliven our souls? How might an ecological theology become a centerpiece of our spiritual care-giving? In this course, we will examine the effects of environmental degradation on the soul, and learn how a co-creation centered theology can stitch back together congregations, families, friendships, and selves.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Francesca Nuzzolese
LC 583 – Spiritual Foundations for the Pastoral Caregiver
This course offers an immersive journey into soulful living and spiritual formation as a foundation for sustainable and effective ministry. Students will explore models of spiritual growth, engage in formative practices, and learn to integrate personal spirituality with pastoral care. Drawing primarily from the Christian tradition while remaining open to other faith practices, the course addresses themes such as identity and vocation, contemplation and action, spirituality and justice, and mourning and celebration. Through lectures, readings, and experiential activities, students will develop essential skills in introspection, theological reflection, compassionate listening, and self-awareness for ministry.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Francesca Nuzzolese
LC 585 – Pastoral Care in the Digital Age
What does care look like in the age of physical distancing? What lessons and practices from this time should we take back to our contexts once we are face to face again? How can technology deepen, rather than distract us from, our pastoral and other care-giving relationships? This course will take a look at how care-givers can employ technology in pastorally sensitive and useful ways, while also being mindful of the risks and problems with losing face to face interaction.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Richard Coble
LC 587 – Pastoral Ministry and Human Trafficking
This course provides an introductory overview of human trafficking, one of the most complex and pervasive global injustices. Drawing on interdisciplinary research and insights from Christian anti-trafficking practitioners, students will examine the systemic forces fueling sex and labor exploitation and explore local manifestations of this phenomenon. The course emphasizes theological reflection and pastoral response, equipping students to craft contextually grounded strategies for prevention and care. Through engagement with literature, lived experience, and practical exercises, participants will develop informed, compassionate approaches to address trafficking as a profound challenge to faith and justice.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Francesca Nuzzolese
LC 588 – Spiritual Formation and Cultural Contexts in Chaplaincy
This course looks through the contexts of Indigenous scholars, activists, poets, and expansive human beings to gather an understanding of spiritual formation through their cultural contexts as a means of identifying intersections of care and compassion.[1] Throughout this course we will investigate areas of convergence and divergence of social, cultural, and other elements as we continue to expound on our ethic of care as spiritual care practitioners.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Tomeka Jacobs
LC 590 – LC Competency Exercise
*Please refer to section 7.1.6-7.1.8 of the Student Handbook*

Prerequisite: Completion of all other LC 500 level work
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Richard Coble
Pastoral Care in a Climate-Traumatized World
This course explores the intersection of pastoral care and climate change, equipping students with the theological, emotional, and practical tools to minister effectively in a post-pandemic world facing an ecological crisis. Students will engage with ecological theology, climate science, and contemporary pastoral practices to understand the spiritual and psychological impacts of climate change on individuals and communities. The course emphasizes trauma-informed care, ecological grief, resilience building, and advocacy through a pastoral lens. Students will learn to offer compassionate, justice-oriented support that fosters hope, healing, and prophetic action in congregational, community, and chaplaincy contexts.

Prerequisite: LC 520
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Beth Toler
LC 669 – Inter-Religious Approaches to Spiritual Care and Chaplaincy
Chaplaincy is more than bedside prayer, however meaningful. In the twenty-first century, chaplaincy has the potential to reach into the ontologies of patients and families for competent and fluid care that impacts throughout time, space, and place. This course looks through the contexts of Indigenous scholars, activists, poets, and expansive human beings to gather an understanding of spiritual formation through their cultural contexts as a means of identifying intersections of care and compassion.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LC 670 – Pastoral Diagnosis
This course will help students to: 1. identify levels of Pastoral Care, 2. develop a diagnostic and pastoral care matrix, 3. identify principles of family systems and 4. identify, develop, and evaluate appropriate pastoral care responses making use of the case study method. The course will address these goals especially through the discussion of case studies in a variety of issues pastors encounter as care-givers. Consideration will also be given to the theological and spiritual dimensions of pastoral diagnosis and care, and to self-care on the part of the pastor.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LC 671 – Short-Term Pastoral Counseling
The course will utilize Narrative Therapy as our primary psycho-therapeutic theory, which will shape our practice of short term pastoral counseling. We’ll begin by exploring the differences between pastoral care, pastoral counseling and psychotherapy, and will consider the importance of negotiating into and out of those different kinds of care.

We’ll then move into the theoretical grounding for narrative therapy, with particular attention to its postmodern commitments, the role of the counselor, how this approach intersects with our theological commitments, several key assumptions related to justice and pathology, and an overview of the counseling process.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LC 672 – Clinical Pastoral Education
*Please refer to section 5.10 of the Student Handbook.*

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LC 673 – Pastoral Care and Substance Abuse
Through this course, the students will explore the psychological, biological, cultural and social dynamics that are present in substance abuse and dependency. Deeper understanding of the different layers of the lived experience of substance abuse, along with rigorous theological reflection, will allow students to develop competency in pastoral care for those who suffer from substance related problems.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LC 674 – Incarnational Ministry: Pastoral Care in Multicultural Contexts
Students in this course will explore the significance of sociocultural contexts in ministry settings. Through a framework informed by incarnational theology, students will develop a reflective and practical approach to caring for cultural diversity in congregations.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LC 675 – Empathy in Pastoral Care & Counseling
This course introduces ministry students to foundational theories, practices, and methods of empathy in pastoral care and counseling. More specifically, it is designed to train seminarians to become attentive to how empathy functions in caregiving practices, and to help them develop critical tools for understanding both the strengths and limitations of empathic caregiving. Students are expected to reflect carefully on their own social location, in order to hone ministry practices that are aware of the limits of their empathy. They will also be challenged to consider how empathic listening gives way to other forms of communal pastoral and political praxis. Special attention is paid to the identities, narratives, and unique vulnerabilities of both givers and recipients of pastoral care—including but not limited to race, gender, sexuality, disability, socio-economic status, and exposure to trauma.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LC 676 – Political Pastoral Theology
This course introduces ministry students to the political dimension of pastoral caregiving and theology. More specifically, it offers seminarians a basic framework for understanding how the theological principles of pastoral care call us to move beyond traditional counseling settings, and into social advocacy and political interventions. This course thus invites students to reflect theologically on the limits of dyadic pastoral counseling (i.e. – one-on-one counseling in an ecclesial setting) and to think constructively about how caregiving must extend to other forms of prophetic witness. Toward this end, students will be required to examine and identify strategies for offering pastoral care to their ecclesial and community setting, which include politically contentious topics. In the process, students are expected to analyze how matters of race, gender, sexuality, disability, and socio-economic status shape our pastoral decisions for political advocacy and witness.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LC 677 – Cross Cultural Perspectives on Death and Dying
This course explores death, dying, and grief as universal yet deeply personal experiences shaped by theology, culture, and social location. Emphasizing cross-cultural awareness and humility, students will examine diverse perspectives on loss and bereavement to cultivate pastoral sensitivity in sacred spaces of mourning. Through theological reflection and practical engagement, the course aims to prepare students to embody a prophetic pastoral presence that honors diversity and responds compassionately to those experiencing loss, particularly where grief is compounded by cultural misunderstanding.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Francesca Nuzzolese
LC 678 – Pastoral Care in Youth Ministry
This course examines spiritual care of adolescents with attention to identity and faith formation. In today’s rapidly shifting world, with the increasing secularization and digitalization of modern life, in the wake of the Black Lives Matter movement and the increasing examination of homophobia and sexism in the church, teenagers are increasingly asking how faith is relevant to their lives. This course will give spiritual care-givers tools to walk alongside teenagers through their faith journeys in this time. We will read from a wide range of authors varying in social location to examine how race, sexuality, and gender shape teenage identity and experiences. Further, we will examine deep case studies of young adult experience through the use of graphic memoirs and young adult novels.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Richard Coble
LC 679 – Caring for a Traumatized World
This course introduces students to Trauma Theory as a lens for understanding the world as deeply impacted by trauma and in need of trauma-informed care. Students will examine the mechanics and effects of trauma on individuals and societies, while critically assessing how institutions and systems often perpetuate harm rather than healing. Through theological reflection and practical engagement, the course equips students to develop trauma-sensitive approaches to ministry and care, fostering resilience and hope in communities marked by suffering.

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Francesca Nuzzolese
Human Trafficking 101: From Insight to Intervention
This course provides a foundational overview of human trafficking, drawing from scholarly research and the real-world experiences of Christian anti-trafficking leaders. It is designed to equip students with the tools to recognize the signs of trafficking locally and globally, and to begin developing a thoughtful, context-sensitive pastoral response. By keeping one ear to the ground—attuned to how trafficking manifests in our own communities—and one eye on the systemic forces that sustain exploitation worldwide, students will be invited into a learning journey that is both academically grounded and pastorally engaged.


Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Francesca Nuzzolese
LC 681 - Inter-faith Pastoral Perspectives on Suffering
For ages humans have turned to various religious traditions and spiritual paths to find meaning and empowerment in the context of suffering. Our growing global society invites and demands that pastoral/spiritual care-givers seek an empathic understanding and respectful engagement of these various traditions and the ideas that stem from them. In this course, the instructor and students will examine human, ecological and cosmic suffering through the lenses of the world’s major religious traditions: Hinduism, Buddhism; Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Students will also cultivate spiritual/pastoral care practices that
sensitively assess and engage suffering in light of the various religions

Prerequisite: Successful completion of one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LC 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Beth Toler
♦ Updated 05/04/26
LF 550 – Biblical and Vocational Foundations of the Teaching Ministry
This course rests on the premise that one of the crucial tasks of those called to be pastors and/or educators is to teach in the church. In this course, we seek an understanding of the teaching ministry as we explore the purpose, context, content, and process of teaching, drawing on biblical and vocational foundations of teaching.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tamar Wasoian
LF 551 – Congregation as Context
“Faith formation is nurtured by the whole life of a congregation, the gathered community of faithful people… Everything that happens in a congregation is part of the process of faith formation” (Diane E. Shallue, p. 4). This course draws upon materials from the field of congregational studies to prepare students to understand the context, culture, and theology of a particular congregation in light of driving forces affecting faith formation in congregations in the United States.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tamar Wasoian
LF 552 – Cultural Shifts Impacting the Teaching of Faith
The culture around us is changing bringing new opportunities for us to teach faith. The church must find ways to be the church in these changing times. In this course we will examine three cultural shifts: digital age, the rise of the SBNR/Nones, and religious pluralism. We will conclude by reconsidering faith formation in light of these cultural shifts.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tamar Wasoian
LF 553 – Stages of Faith
The theme that unites this course is that different people experience, understand, and live their faith in different ways. We begin by reflecting on the nature of faith in the scripture. Then we look at faith development theories of James Fowler and John Westerhoff, which help us understand developmentally how people may experience faith at different times in their lives. We then look at some best practices in faith formation to see what we might learn about growing in faith.


Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tamar Wasoian
LF 564 – New Building Bridges of Understanding Regarding Human Sexuality
Human sexuality continues to be a contentious topic within theological discourse, shaping ecclesial debates on issues ranging from the ordination of women to the full participation of queer folx in the life of the church. Regardless of a student’s personal beliefs, this course equips students with tools for engaging difficult conversations in ways that cultivate deeper understanding across differing perspectives. Drawing on concepts such as rhetorical theology, working gospel, and moral worldview, students will learn to analyze how theological arguments about sexuality are constructed and communicated within religious communities. The primary goal of the course is to prepare students to engage issues of human sexuality thoughtfully, critically, and intentionally in the practice of ministry.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Nicole McDonald
LF 565: Lectio Divina: Scripture in Catholic Spirituality
How can careful biblical interpretation lead to deeper prayer and spiritual transformation? This course introduces the ancient Christian practice of Lectio Divina while integrating contemporary biblical scholarship and close, attentive readings of Scripture. Students will explore monastic traditions of scriptural prayer, Ignatian contemplation, and pastoral uses of Scripture in preaching, counseling, and spiritual direction. Attention will also be given to the movement from critical analysis to contemplative encounter, showing how study and prayer mutually enrich one another. Designed for students from diverse Christian traditions, the course demonstrates how rigorous engagement with the biblical text can nourish a sacramental imagination—a concept rooted in Catholic theology—to cultivate a living encounter with the Word of God in ministry, community life, and daily practice.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Michael Matlock
LF 566 – Early Christian Spiritualites
This course explores age-appropriate approaches to teaching and learning in ministry with children in the 21st century. Students will examine challenges facing children’s ministry today and consider its role within home, community, and church. Through reflection on personal learning experiences, participants will study age-specific faith formation, family and community learning, and inclusive worship practices. The course emphasizes creative strategies for engaging children and fostering intergenerational participation, equipping students to design educational ministries that nurture faith and belonging for all ages.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tomeka Jacobs
LF 567 – Spiritual Practices and Guiding Frameworks
Early church spirituality has greatly influenced post-modern Christian spirituality. Spiritual practices and guiding frameworks are tools and systems that individuals or communities use to cultivate a deeper connection with their spiritual beliefs, values, and experiences. This course looks at spiritual practices and guiding frameworks from early Church and Medieval mothers and fathers in the fourth and eleventh centuries.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tomeka Jacobs
LF 568 – Introduction to Spiritual Formation
Spiritual formation is the path of becoming and arriving through a continuum of contemplation, curiosity, creativity, and compassion. Through critical engagement and analysis this course is designed to deepen one’s spiritual journey and foster personal growth and transformation.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tomeka Jacobs
LF 570 – Children's Ministry in the Church
This course examines age-appropriate approaches to teaching and learning in ministry with children in today’s changing context. Students will explore challenges facing children’s ministry and its role within home, community, and church. Through reflection on personal learning experiences, participants will study age-specific faith formation, family and community learning, and inclusive worship practices. The course emphasizes creative strategies for engaging children and fostering intergenerational participation, equipping students to design educational ministries that nurture faith and belonging for all ages.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tomeka Jacobs
LF 572 – Teaching the Bible
In this course we examine a time-honored and common practice of faith formation in congregations: Bible study. We consider why congregations engage in Bible study and what conditions need to be present in order to help children, youth, and adults learn best. We also explore a variety of methods that can be used to design a Bible study, as well as strategies to help people engage the Bible in their prayer lives.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tamar Wasoian
LF 575 – Storied Learning
Storytelling is as old as the human existence in the world. Through stories our brain and our consciousness explore and make sense of the world in which we exist in. Through stories that we tell about our lives, we create a world that makes sense to us. Stories about our faith and faithfulness not only speak of our past experiences but also construct our daily realities and future hopes. This course will be looking at literature about stories and narrative as means for learning and being. Because Christian education is focused on faithful living, connecting story, self and the Divine is an important method in effective teaching and learning ministry of the church. This class will help the students design their own ministry experience using collaborative storytelling as creative teaching and learning method.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tamar Wasoian
LF 577 – Special Topics in Youth Ministry: Baptism and Confirmation
This is an advanced course in faith formation, specifically focused upon issues of the pastoral practice of baptism and confirmation with teens.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Christopher Rodkey
LF 579 – Faith Formation in Adolescent Women
In this course, we begin by considering the context of adolescent women, naming developmental issues faced by young women and common cultural narratives about girlhood identity to which they are exposed. We then examine themes that arise in research about the faith lives of adolescent women and consider what this research implies for ministry with adolescent women. Finally, we look closely at methods used in religious education with adolescent women to support their faith formation, including girlfriend theology groups and transformative prayer practices.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tamar Wasoian
LF 581 – Holistic Education
This course explores holistic education as an approach to integrating mind, body, soul, and community in relation to God’s vision of wholeness. Students will engage practices that foster personal well-being and vocational integrity, including physical and mental meditation, journaling, and theological reflection. Themes of fullness of life, integrity of creation, and holiness in ministry will guide class discussions. Drawing on diverse readings and experiential learning, students will design a holistic ministry project as a final assignment, equipping them to promote wholeness and spiritual depth in their own contexts.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tamar Wasoian
LF 582 – The Spirituality of Public Spaces
This course examines the public dimension of spirituality as expressed in communal action and shared spaces. Inspired by movements from Tahrir Square to Charlottesville, students will explore how faith communities redefine spirituality by bringing it from private sanctuaries into public witness. Through reflection on personal experiences and analysis of contemporary examples, the course considers how public expressions of faith challenge traditional understandings and inform ministry practices. Participants will develop strategies for integrating this vision of public spirituality into teaching and leadership within their own contexts.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tamar Wasoian
LF 583 – Adult Spirituality
This course explores aspects of age appropriate teaching and learning ministry with adults. Moving through life spans brings new challenges to already existing realities of life. This course highlights these challenges and places ministry with adults in the sphere of home and community as well as the church. In the first part of this class, we will be reflecting on the work of James W. Fowler and learn about faith formation in adulthood. We will be reflecting on vocation, grace, and the journey of being and becoming. In the second part, we will be learning from Linda J. Vogel about her vision of education that answers the age appropriate needs of the adult learners and practical road map to achieve such vision.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tamar Wasoian
LF 584 – Feminist Pedagogy
This course examines the intersection of body, gender, and teaching/learning within the context of religious education. Moving beyond stereotypical gender conversations, students will explore how embodied and gendered experiences shape learning patterns and ministry practices. Through feminist pedagogical perspectives and education theories, the course envisions renewed approaches to ministry that affirm women’s spiritual and educational needs while inviting all genders into the conversation. Participants will reflect critically on androcentric assumptions in education and develop strategies for inclusive, holistic learning that empowers faithful living.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Tamar Wasoian
LF 588 - IFS: Psychospiritual Approach to Healing and Transformation
Internal Family Systems Model (IFS) is a contemplative, soulful, and non-pathologizing approach to personal healing and spiritual transformation. This course, taught by a trained and certified IFS practitioner, introduces students to the core concepts and practices of the model, places the model into dialogue with contemplative spiritual traditions, and adapts the model as an accessible and uniquely liberating pathway toward psycho-spiritual wholeness and social reconciliation rooted in empowered compassion.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Tomeka Jacobs
LF 590 – Competency Exercise
*Please refer to section 7.1.6-7.1.8 of the Student Handbook*

Prerequisite: Completion of all other LF 500 level work
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Narola McFayden
LF 670 – Liberative Pedagogies and Practices
This course explores liberative and critical pedagogies as a foundation for educational ministry. Beginning with theological and anthropological questions about human identity and the need for liberation, students will engage Paulo Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed and its influence on secular and religious education. The course examines narrative, aesthetic, and embodied pedagogies that promote critical thought and action, concluding with theological reflection on faith’s role in liberative teaching. Students will practice discernment as a spiritual discipline for aligning educational ministry with God’s transformative work in the world.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LF 671 – Christian Adaptation of Spiritual Practices
This course equips students to lead congregations through healthy change in spiritual practices. After studying how churches across history have adapted practices, students will develop collaborative guidelines for evaluating current practices in light of biblical norms, denominational models, and cultural context. The course emphasizes discernment—deciding which practices to retain, modify, or discontinue—and planning experimental changes with congregational input. Through practical exercises, students will learn strategies for fostering shared ownership, evaluating outcomes, and guiding communities toward deeper growth in Christ.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LF 672 – Who is My Neighbor?
As pastors and educators, we are tasked with the responsibility to nurture Christlikeness in those who identify themselves as followers of Jesus Christ. To be a faithful disciple of Jesus Christ is to love our neighbors as Christ taught us. To be neighborly we mush understand ourselves and the "neighbor." In this course, we will seek answers to the question, "Who is my neighbor?" by first reflecting on our own faith; and second, learning about our neighbor's faith. We then will examine how living out our faith will lead us to be the neighbor Christ calls us to be.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Narola McFayden
LF 673 – Thomas Merton: His Life, Spirituality and Social Consciousness
This course is designed to introduce students to the life, spirituality and social awareness of the renowned Trappist monk, Thomas Merton. It will do so via three interlocking approaches. The first will focus on Merton’s life, noting the important people and events that were formative for his spirituality, and helped shape his ministry as spiritual director and author. The second focus will be on Merton’s spirituality, reviewing not only on how his life influenced his spiritual formation, but also on how his studies of other faiths also influenced him. The third focus will be on the development and growth of his spiritual consciousness and how these influenced his commitment to social issues, even as he lived the life of a cloistered contemplative monk.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Williams Grimes
LF 674 – Development of Spirituality in Later Life
This course examines the spiritual and cognitive dimensions of later life, focusing on how aging shapes existential questions and faith development. Students will explore changes in brain function, modes of thinking, and evolving approaches to spirituality, from certainty to reflective openness. Drawing on developmental theory and theological reflection, the course addresses how these processes influence meaning-making, legacy, and hope. Practical strategies will equip students to support individuals and communities in navigating later-life challenges, fostering pastoral care that honors maturity, complexity, and spiritual depth.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. John Cavanaugh
LF 675 – Creating a Beloved Community with Youth
Young people’s trust in religious institutions continues to decline. What might we as followers of Jesus Christ and as members of a Christian community do to show young people that we are here for them and that they are loved? In this course, we will examine what makes a community beloved (the term “beloved community” was popularized by Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.), what we could do to create a beloved community with youth (instead of “for” youth) and imagine possibilities for creating a beloved community in our particular context.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Narola McFayden
LF 676 – Creation Spiritualities
This course examines theological perspectives on the human condition and pathways to life in the Spirit through two major traditions: Augustine’s concept of Original Sin and the Neoplatonic stages of purgation, illumination, and contemplation, and the Creation Spirituality approach emphasizing Original Blessing and the fourfold path—Via Positiva, Negativa, Creativa, and Transformativa. Students will explore the roots of Creation Spirituality in Catholic mysticism, theology, and contemporary thought, and consider its connections to Indigenous spiritualities, ecotheology, feminist and liberation theologies. The course invites critical reflection on how these frameworks shape faith and practice today.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. John Cavanaugh
LF 677 – Thomas Merton: Witness to Peace
The Roman Catholic Trappist monk and spiritual writer Thomas Merton (1915-1968) is widely celebrated as one of the most important religious figures of the 20th century. This seminar offers an intensive engagement with Merton’s autobiographical and spiritual writings as well as his prophetic social essays on war and peace, race relations, interfaith dialogue, and communion with God through the natural world. It is hoped that students will not just “study” Merton critically but will be invited to engage his writings personally and holistically, “through the eyes of the heart,” and further to consider the enduring pastoral implications of Merton’s witness to Christian faith and critical social engagement in our times.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Chris Pramuk
LF 678 – Narrative Pedagogy
Storytelling is an ancient epistemology. It is through storytelling cultures have maintained and built identities. This course is a study of the use of the narrative arts—storytelling, creative writing, playmaking, spiritual autobiography, improvisational role-plays, and dramatic presentations—as a means for religious education, theological reflection, spiritual growth, and social empowerment. We will explore the dimensions of narrative pedagogy through the works of Alice Walker and Alexis Pauline Gumbs.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LF 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Tomeka Jacobs
LF 680 – Listening and Imagining: Spiritual Practices to Cultivate Just Communities
This course brings together the resources of spiritual practice, theology, and traditions of social change to help us listen the ways God is at work in our shared lives and to imagine how we might collaboratively work for a better future. We will study and engage in practices of listening that seek to deepen one’s relationship with God, heal and thicken relationships, and build cooperation with grassroots communities. In tandem with these spiritual exercises, we will pursue processes that creatively and collectively engage the prophetic imagination through the power of symbol and story. Bringing these two trajectories together, we will begin to discern and experiment with how the symbols and stories that currently animate our communities might be enlivened, expanded, or transformed for the work of cultivating justice and joy.

Credits: 2.0
Prerequisites: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LF 500 level work
Faculty: Wilson Dickinson
♦ Updated 06/05/26
LM 520 – Program Planning and Evaluation
A congregation’s ministry programs are the most prominent outward signs of its purpose and identity. Planning them with clarity and evaluating them with care will not necessarily save or transform a congregation, but good planning and evaluation ensure that congregations offer programs that matter to people and to God. By taking this course, students will learn how to lead others into effective processes of program planning and evaluation in their congregations. In the last week of the course, students will apply the same processes to the completion of their LTS degree/certificate and thus learn one way of discerning their vocation.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
LM 540 - Manejo de Proyecto y Capacidad Eclesial para Accion Transformativo
Manejo de Proyecto y Capacidad Eclesial para Acción Transformativo" es un curso integral diseñado para equipar a los estudiantes con las habilidades esenciales de gestión de proyectos necesarias para impulsar proyectos impactantes y transformadores dentro de contextos eclesiales. Este curso integra los principios de gestión de proyectos con la misión eclesial, proporcionando un marco único para la planificación. , ejecutar y evaluar proyectos que fomenten el crecimiento comunitario y el desarrollo espiritual. A través de una combinación de conocimientos teóricos y aplicaciones prácticas, los estudiantes aprenderán a desarrollar estatutos de proyectos, establecer objetivos SMART, involucrar a las partes interesadas, gestionar riesgos y medir el desempeño del proyecto utilizando métodos cualitativos y cuantitativos.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
LM 541 – Project Management and Ecclesial Capacity for Transformative Action
Project Management and Ecclesial Capacity for Transformative Action" is a comprehensive course designed to equip students with the essential project management skills needed to drive impactful and transformative projects within ecclesial contexts. This course integrates project management principles with ecclesial mission, providing a unique framework for planning, executing, and evaluating projects that foster community growth and spiritual development. Through a blend of theoretical knowledge and practical application, students will learn to develop project charters, set SMART goals, engage stakeholders, manage risks, and measure project performance using both qualitative and quantitative methods.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
LM 556 - Living the Catholic Experience: Sharing Our Stories
As students approach the completion of their studies and prepare for their practicum and final project, this course provides the necessary time to reflect on their overall learning and experiences during their program as they prepare for what is next. Using narrative and storytelling, this course will focus on three primary goals: (1) a critical reflection on the overall learning experience from their program, (2) consideration of what is next in terms of each student’s practicum, and (3) a plan for their final project that prepares them for their future careers. This course is an opportunity to demonstrate the values and beliefs of the Catholic experience and to develop their own compelling story as to how they live this experience.

Prerequisite: None
Faculty
Credits: 1.0
LM 557 – Tech Basics for Pastors and Congregational Life
This course explores how the COVID-19 pandemic reshaped technology use in worship spaces, prompting pastors and church leaders to adopt unfamiliar tools to reach homebound members and expand their ministry online. Participants will learn the basics of streaming, equipment selection, and digital outreach strategies to support both in-person and virtual congregations. The course addresses common questions raised during the pandemic and offers practical guidance for integrating technology into worship. Ultimately, it aims to show how digital tools can foster community and help congregations extend their reach beyond the physical church building.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Prof. Dominique Highfil
LM 558 – Perspectives of Bi-Vocational Ministry
Bi-vocational ministers—those who serve congregations while holding other paid employment—play a vital yet often overlooked role in U.S. Protestant churches, particularly in rural, immigrant, and historically marginalized communities. This two-week course examines current research on bi-vocational ministry, highlighting its challenges, benefits, and strategic use in church planting. Students will engage with the lived experiences of bi-vocational ministers and the congregations they serve, gaining insight into the dynamics of this model. The course provides tools for understanding its implications and encourages participants to reflect on how bi-vocational ministry might inform their own pastoral leadership.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Kristen Bentley
LM 560 – Resources for Mission: Stewardship as Vision and Practice
This course will provide a basic Biblical, theological, and practical introduction into the spiritual discipline of stewardship and provide best practice principles for guiding the financial and fiduciary responsibilities of the pastor as church leader.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Prof. Bruce Barkhauer
LM 561 – Governance & Management
Governance and Management (LM 561), along with Stewardship (LM 560) and Conflict (LM 562), forms the trio of required courses for the Leading the Church into Mission curriculum. Taken together, these courses help prepare you to provide management and leadership for congregations, especially congregations confronting change.

This course builds on LM 520 to help students lead congregations through adaptive change. It explores governance structures, the roles of boards and volunteer teams, and strategies for equipping members for ministry. Students assess their own congregational systems and learn to distinguish between technical and adaptive change, as well as management and leadership, to better support mission-focused transformation.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0 (Offered during On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Rev. Dr. Denise Bell
LM 562 – Managing Congregational Conflict
Conflict (LM 562), along with Administration and Property (LM 561) and Stewardship (LM 560), forms the trio of required courses for the Leading the Church into Mission curriculum. Taken together, these courses help prepare you to provide management and leadership for congregations, especially congregations confronting change.

Building on LM 520, this course equips students to lead congregations through conflict during times of change. It explores the connections between conflict, loss, and grief, and offers strategies for identifying tensions and supporting those affected. Students learn to distinguish types of conflict and apply appropriate leadership responses. The course also invites theological and liturgical reflection on conflict, helping leaders use the past to shape a faithful and resilient congregational future.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0 (Offered during On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Rev. Dr. Denise Bell
LM 563- Evangelism and Outreach
This course challenges quick-fix approaches to Stewardship and Evangelism, arguing they are deeply rooted in discipleship and spiritual formation. Rather than relying on programmatic solutions, students will explore how these areas reflect a congregation’s theological depth and spiritual health. Through critical reflection, the course invites participants to rethink traditional strategies and consider how renewed commitment to discipleship can foster authentic growth in both church membership and financial stewardship.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Prof. Bruce Barkhauer
LM 566 – Pastor as Administrator/Chief Operating Officer
While one often thinks of pastors as “spiritual leaders,” this course aims to provide congregational and theological perspectives on the role of the pastor as administrator and chief operating officer of the corporation, and its implications.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Donald Gillett
LM 567 – Themes in Global Mission
In a rapidly changing world, this course challenges outdated approaches to cross-cultural mission. Students explore key themes in the church’s mission through diverse global perspectives, especially from the Global South. By examining theological and ethical assumptions, participants gain tools to help local churches engage in domestic and international mission rooted in partnership, mutuality, and justice-centered relationships. The course fosters deeper understanding and equips students for mission practices relevant to today’s context.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Jonathan Barnes
LM 568 – Mission and Migration in an Uneven World
Due to the myriad effects of globalization, students engage in mission and ministry in an uneven and fragmented world. Furthermore, many local churches where students currently (or will) serve view mission in this uneven world, whether local or global, in terms of what the North American church does “to” or “for” others. This course will assist in unmasking our own ethical/theological presuppositions concerning globalization and migration, as well as giving students basic analytic and interpretive skills in assisting local churches to move from a charity model of mission to one centered on solidarity and mutuality; a model of ministry “with” others.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Jonathan Barnes
LM 570 – Sustaining the Call of Ecclesia: Administration in Times of Crisis
This course invites students to explore the difference between sustaining a church and sustaining the call to be church. Through strategic planning and theological reflection, students examine church models, resource allocation, and the impact of capitalism on ministry priorities. Emphasizing justice and equity, the course equips participants with interpretive frameworks and practical skills to discern their congregation’s calling amid social, spiritual, and fiscal challenges, fostering faithful engagement with God’s kin-dom on Earth.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Yara Gonzalez
LM 573 – Funding Special Ministries
This course aims to provide practical resources for clergy in securing external grant funds to support their ministries.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Donald Gillett
LM 574 – Building Communities from the Inside Out: The Church and Community Development
Humanitarianism and development have long been part of the Western Christian response to poverty and relief work. However, in a context of globalization, migration, and growing inequalities within the United States, skills and practices that focus on empowerment and utilizing community assets can and should be applied to this work, including in one’s local context.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Jon Barnes

LM 586 – Mission as Dialogue: Faith in a Pluralistic World
This course explores Christian mission in a pluralistic world shaped by migration and global Christianity. Students examine theologies of pluralism and practices of mission as dialogue, engaging with voices from multi-faith contexts. Emphasizing deep listening, mutual learning, and transformation, the course equips participants to help local churches approach mission in ways that honor religious diversity and foster justice-centered relationships across faith lines.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Jonathan Barnes
LM 587 – Developing Green Congregations
This course equips students to lead congregations in environmental justice, climate action, and Creation care. Students will explore eco-anxiety, resilience, and the spiritual dimensions of ecological work while learning to communicate climate science effectively. Using an assessment tool, they’ll evaluate their organization’s engagement and design a context-specific final project. Through readings, discussions, and eco-spiritual practices, students will develop the knowledge, skills, and emotional grounding needed to foster sustainable, justice-centered ministry in a time of ecological crisis.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade and Prof. Carol Devine
LM 588 – Holistic Estate Planning
You get the final say – but what do your final wishes say about you and your values, your faith, and your priorities? What does your preparation for death, say about your life?

The purpose of this course is to examine some of these important “end of life” questions from a holistic perspective of biblical and theologically sound faith.



Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
LM 589 – The Art of Flourishing in Ministry
This course's main aim delves into the concept of flourishing in both personal and communal aspects of
life and ministry, independent of ministry performance and evaluation metrics. The course will further apply
concepts of flourishing to the life of the course participants, allowing them to view it as a personal and
collective investment such that they may be willing to explore for themselves practices cultivating healthy and
sustaining relationships to transform lives.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Rev. Dr. Denise Bell
LM 590 – LM Competency Exercise
*Please refer to section 7.1.6-7.1.8 of the Student Handbook*

Prerequisite: Completion of all other LM 500 level work
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
LM 591 - Wholistic Finances and Stewardship
This course is designed to understand fundraising as a ministry. It will provide the perspectives of biblical stewardship; insights on creating generous congregants and constituents; and explore the practical steps in crafting a theology of development. This course is designed for lay leaders, ordained clergy, fundraisers and developers of nonprofit faith based organizations and institutions.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
LM 592 - Becoming the Pastor
Becoming the pastor of a particular community of faith is a shared journey that integrates the pastor's theological understanding of God's call, the pastor's sense of self, and the congregation's human and spiritual identity. It involves navigating the multiplicity of self as person, pastor, and participant in the world, including one's calling and the specific place and time of a faith community. One of the significant challenges and rewards for someone who accepts the role of senior pastor or pastoral staff in a church setting is to continually present themselves as a whole, evolving person, with a readiness to invite others to participate in collective growth and spiritual transformation, strengthening the church to serve the Lord and the world. The engagement between the pastor and the people is like a dance, where partners move in sync, lead, follow, and communicate interchangeably, caught in the tension between being led by the Spirit and congregational, community, and personal circumstances.
LM 593 - From Soil to Soul: Mission and Community Transformation
"Tend the soil. Serve the city. Transform the Church. A four-week journey from Amos and Luke to your own community garden."

What if the soil beneath your feet held the seeds of the Church's renewal? In this four-week graduate course, you will explore the Church's missional vocation through the integrative lens of food justice, prophetic witness, and community transformation. Designed for a mixed cohort of clergy, graduate students, and lay leaders, the course is anchored in Rev. Dr. Michael L. Zachary's From Soil to Soul: The Impact of Community Gardens on Food Insecurity. Together, you will engage the prophetic ethics of Amos and the liberative gospel of Luke, discerning how Scripture summons today's Church to confront food insecurity, structural inequity, and ecological crisis. Guided by Charles Wesley's charge "to serve this present age," you will cultivate a forward-looking missiology and design justice-rooted ministries that embody the kingdom of God in the soil of your own community.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor:: Rev. Dr. Michael Zachary
LM 628 – Issues in Church Administration
This course equips students with practical skills and insight for effective church administration and leadership. Through readings, peer dialogue, and projects, students will explore governance models, conflict management, and congregational mapping to assess and restructure administrative systems. Emphasizing wisdom and agility, the course prepares ministers to navigate diverse challenges and lead congregations with clarity and purpose. Participants will gain tools to understand how power flows and how to foster healthier organizational practices.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Donald Gillett
LM 670 – The Ethics of Pastoral Leadership
This course explores the ethical dimensions of pastoral leadership, emphasizing moral discernment alongside strategic skills. Students examine how virtues like honesty, justice, and fidelity shape decisions in governance, stewardship, fundraising, personnel management, evangelism, and public ministry. Through case studies and critical reflection, the course addresses ethical challenges that arise in leadership and congregational practices, helping students develop a thoughtful approach to ministry that supports both individual integrity and communal mission.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LM 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LM 671 – Character and Leadership
Many courses in pastoral leadership are about the ‘what’ and ‘how’ of leadership. This one is about the ‘who’ of leadership. Who is a leader? What shapes their character and style as leaders? Factors include class, gender, race and ethnicity, personality type, emotional intelligence, and spiritual type. What kind of leader are you becoming? In this course you will be invited to be self-reflective about how the above-named factors shape your own leadership style. You will also practice the skill of conducting relational meetings with other potential leaders, in order to identify and cultivate their leadership. Finally, you will receive feedback on your leadership style from members of your congregation.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LM 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LM 672 – Church Administration & Property
Many pastors say that they weren’t called into ministry in order to read balance sheets, run meetings, and conduct background checks. At the same time, many pastors say they wish they’d learned how to do these things in seminary. Here is your chance. This course will prepare you to lead congregations as effective managers of people, programs, and property.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LM 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LM 673 – Culturally Attentive Conflict Ministry
This course equips students to lead congregations through conflict with wisdom and cultural sensitivity. Building on prior LM coursework, it uses a dialogical, problem-based approach to explore conflict detection, diagnosis, and response. Students examine leadership postures—environmental, ecological, and evocational—while considering the risks of iatrogenic harm and the importance of cultural context. Through shared learning, students develop practical skills and theological insight for navigating conflict in ways that foster healing, justice, and congregational discernment.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LM 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LM 676 - Ghana Pilgrimage Trip
The Pilgrimage to Ghana Travel Seminar is an expression of LTS’s commitment to the formation of students, clergy, and lay leaders who embody a deep understanding of our global realities, the interconnections of our lives, and the mission of the global church. The pilgrimage provides an opportunity to study the exponential grown of Christianity in sub-Saharan Africa, the efforts and challenges of contextualizing the gospel as an authentic expression of African faith and spirituality, and the opportunities and challenges currently facing theological education in the Ghanian context. There will also be opportunity to visit community-based projects of the Christian Council of Ghana related to interfaith dialogue, human trafficking, and economic justice.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% LM 500 work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Jonathan Barnes
LM 677 – Mission in the 21st Century: Justice, Mutuality, and Partnership
Despite our rapidly changing context, both locally and globally, many Christians continue to use inherited and antiquated understandings and practices when engaging in cross-cultural mission.

This course will explore the changing perceptions of the church’s nature and mission, and the implications for ecumenicism, interfaith dialogue, evangelism, and justice work. Through exposure to a variety of voices and perspectives, including those from the Global South, students will better understand their own theological/ethical presuppositions around mission as well as gain knowledge and skills to assist local churches in approaching both domestic and international mission through a lens of partnership, mutuality and justice centered relationships.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LM 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Jonathan Barnes
LM 678 – Congregational Systems
A congregation is much more than the sum of its individual parts. It is an emotional system with a multi-faceted history (subsystems) that: drives its decisions; defines its culture and its relationship to its community; and, determines its relationship with its pastoral leadership. In this course the student will be given tools to better understand the systemic dynamics of congregations and how to define themselves and their leadership styles within any congregational system for effective ministry.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LM 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LM 679 - Reimagining Religion and Mission
The categorizing of "religion" as a separate sphere of life from the "secular," as well as its use in identifying various systems of belief or commitment, is a distinctly modern phenomenon. In this class we will discuss the notion of "religion" as a modern concept, deconstructing its usage and discussing the impact this has on mission, the contextualization of Christianity in various cultures, and interfaith dialogue and relationships.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LM 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Esther S. Parajuli & Dr. Jonathan Barnes
♦ Updated 03/30/26
LW 540 - Adoracion y Predicacion en el Contexto Latinx
Uno de los elementos más importantes en las tradiciones de iglesias Latinas es la predicación. El reformador Martín Lutero consideraba la proclamación de la Palabra la razón principal por la cual se reunían los feligreses a adorar, pues a través de la Palabra proclamada, Cristo emanaba y entraba a los corazones de los oyentes. Este curso tiene tres propósitos principales: 1) revisar los elementos que destacan a la predicación u “homilética” como propiamente “Latina,” 2) conocer algunas voces de predicadores/as destacados de la comunidad Latine y sus contribuciones, y 3) examinar cómo se entrelaza la predicación con la adoración y la vida litúrgica general de la iglesia.
LW 541 - Worship and Preaching in the Black Church
This course explores the liturgical, homiletical, and theological traditions of the African American church, emphasizing its diversity and depth. Students engage liberation and womanist theologies, study distinctive preaching styles, and examine the historical and spiritual dimensions of Black worship. Through reflection and practice, they critically engage the multifaceted nature of African American faith. As a capstone, students will learn and apply a preaching method developed by an African American preacher in a brief sermon.

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
LW 550 – Introduction to Worship
This is a four-week, 1-credit course that is a prerequisite for all other courses in the LW area (Leading the Church in Worship). Students will master basic concepts and theological issues that will provide the foundation for future LW courses. In this course, students will learn the following:

• A basic understanding of ritual, symbol, and worship
• A broad overview of the biblical and historical foundations of Christian worship
• A beginning theology of Christian worship and proclamation
• A broad overview of sacred and liturgical time in the church
• Issues related to leadership in worship, including structuring the liturgical year and designing a basic worship service
• The origins and use of lectionaries
• An introduction to leading public prayer
• An introduction to choosing music for the liturgy

Prerequisite: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 552 – Congregational Song
In this course, students learn the history and theology of congregational singing as a significant element of Christian liturgy and gain practical skills for choosing congregational music for worship. The course is oriented toward students with minimal musical training. This course is a two-week (.5 credit), self-standing module. “Self-standing” means students work through the material independently and at their own pace (as long as all material is completed by 6:00 pm ET on the Saturday of the second week.

Prerequisite: LW 550
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Faculty
LW 553 – Christian Rites and Rituals: Baptism, Communion, Weddings, Funerals (formerly New Birth to Dying in Christ)
This is a four-week (1 credit) course that introduces students to the history, theology, and leadership of Christian sacraments/ordinances and rites of passage. In this course students will become familiar with the following:
• Socio-religious theoretical perspective on the function of worship rituals and rites of passage.
• Biblical, historical, and theological foundations for sacraments/ordinances and Christian rites of passage.
• Detailed understanding of the major rituals of baptism, communion, weddings, and funerals, including biblical, historical, and theological background, as well as practical considerations. The course will also include an ecotheological perspective for understanding the sacraments/ordinances, weddings, and funerals within the context of God’s Creation.

Prerequisite: LW 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 554 – Sermon Preparation
This course will introduce students to the basic content, elements, methods, and forms of preaching, with the goal of moving from biblical exegesis to theological public proclamation.
