Students will learn how to write Central Question, Central Claim, and Central Purpose statements to guide their sermon process. We will also attend to the performance of preaching, including the use of one’s body, presence, and voice in order to deliver effective, engaging, and inspiring sermons.

Prerequisites: LW 550, IF 552, IS 560
Credit: 2.0 (Offered during On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 556 – Forming Sermon Feedback Groups: Sacred Listening and Reflection
This online course equips preachers to form and equip sermon feedback groups that foster sacred listening and meaningful reflection, benefiting both the preacher and sermon listeners. Students will begin by reflecting on their own experiences of giving and receiving feedback with the goal of removing barriers and opening pathways for shared growth. We’ll then move to learning structures, strategies, and techniques to elicit substantive, constructive feedback from sermon listeners. The goal is to train sermon listeners to go beyond superficial responses toward deepened biblical and theological engagement. The course emphasizes creating a culture of deep listening where participants can offer respectful yet robust responses, enabling preachers to grow in their ministry with their community to respond more fully to God’s word together.

Prerequisite: LW 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 574 – Preaching in the Purple Zone
In a time of deep political division, this course equips students to preach and lead with courage, care, and clarity. It explores the challenges clergy face when addressing public issues and introduces “deliberative dialogue” as a method for fostering civil discourse and shared values. Students will learn to help congregations engage respectfully across political differences, navigate “hot topics” with theological integrity, and respond faithfully to God’s Word in a fractured cultural landscape.

NOTE: This course requires students to participate in a synchronous online deliberative dialogue session. The instructor will contact students before the course begins to determine the most ideal day and time for this 75-minute session. This course also requires students to “practice preach” one sermon and submit it along with the manuscript.

Prerequisite: LW 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 576 – Imagination in Preaching
The student will be introduced to a unique aspect of preaching that deals with the use of imagination. Imagination is to be understood as the use of rhetorical tools to make one’s thoughts as true to life as possible, as concrete as possible, and as colorful and as clear as words can make truth.

Prerequisite: LW 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christopher Davis
LW 577 – Practice Preaching
This course is designed to allow students the opportunity to practice and improve skills learned in Sermon Preparation (LW554), in which students received an introductory understanding of scripture, theology, and the practice of preaching. Discussions of the sermon will deal with the full breadth of topics addressed in Sermon Preparation—exegesis; theological claims; the Central Statements (Central Question, Central Claim, Central Purpose); sermon forms; beginnings, transitions, and endings; imagery; and delivery.

Note: This course meets synchronously online for four sessions. Each student will record themselves “practice preaching” one sermon and upload the video for fellow students and the instructor to watch. Each student will have one of the slots during the sessions to discuss their sermon and receive feedback.

MDiv students are required take Practice Preaching once but may take the course as many times as they want throughout their time at LTS.

Prerequisites: LW 550, LW 554
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 578 – Creation-Crisis Preaching and Worship
This course equips students to preach and lead worship in response to environmental devastation and ecological injustice. Emphasizing Creation-centered liturgy, students will learn to design contextually relevant services that reflect the beauty and fragility of God’s world. With attention to geography, culture, and politics, the course fosters an environmentally literate approach to preaching that names ecological realities while proclaiming hope through Christ’s “eco-resurrection.” Students will develop theological and practical tools for faithful, justice-oriented worship.

Prerequisites: LW 550
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 580 – Proclamation and Song
In this course students will examine how preaching may be blended with song to increase effectiveness in proclaiming the Gospel. The course examines specific aspects of preaching theory that deal with the Focus and Function of the sermon. Music is not limited to any specific genre. We will look at a number of criteria for selecting songs for the purpose of enriching preaching. The course is designed to help preachers, pastors, church musicians, and other worship leaders make the most of the mutually beneficial relationship between the Word spoken and sung. The various congregational contexts represented by students in this class will be important to our discussions.

Prerequisite: LW 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Catherine Williams
LW 581 – Digitally Mediated Worship
This course explores the evolving role of technology in Christian worship, from early digital adoption to the widespread shift online during COVID-19. Students will examine theological and practical arguments for and against digitally mediated worship, including responses to public health mandates and civil disobedience. The course equips students with tools to analyze, design, and implement online worship services, fostering thoughtful engagement with the opportunities and challenges of leading faith communities in digital contexts.

Prerequisite: LW 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty

LW 582 – Congregational Music, Identity, and Postcoloniality
This course examines congregational music in postcolonial Caribbean and Latin American churches as a theological and cultural reflection. Students explore how music articulates understandings of God shaped by nationality, gender, and religious identity in contexts marked by colonization. Topics include appropriation, globalization, and the prophetic role of music in resisting colonial and globalizing forces. Through critical engagement, students will assess how congregational music fosters justice-oriented faith and identity in the 21st-century postcolonial church.

Prerequisite: LW 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
LW 583 – Preaching with Contextual Intelligence
This course trains students to exegete various types of listeners in today’s culturally-changing church context for the purpose of effective sermon construction and delivery. Students will obtain theoretical and practical methods to begin exploring a number of sub-cultures that exist within congregations and to learn how to preach biblically and culturally-informed sermons to listeners who come from diverse cultural backgrounds and life situations.

Prerequisite: LW 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Christopher Davis
LW 584 - Holistic Preaching: Methods of Embodiment
This course introduces students to embodied preaching, rooted in the homiletical style of Jesus of Nazareth. Integrating mind, body, and spirit, students engage experiential learning practices—including performing arts techniques, contemplative prayer, and scripture reading—to deepen sermon preparation and delivery. Emphasizing holistic formation, the course equips students to proclaim God’s word with authenticity and presence, cultivating preaching that is spiritually grounded, physically expressive, and theologically rich.

Prerequisities: None
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
LW 590 – LW Competency Exercise
*Please refer to section 7.1.6-7.1.8 of the Student Handbook*

Prerequisite: Completion of all other LW 500 level work
Credit: 0.5
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 591 - Preparing Sermons for a Climate Challenged World
This course equips students to preach the gospel amid environmental devastation and ecological injustice. Emphasizing Creation-centered sermons, students will explore how to name ecological realities with honesty and creativity while proclaiming hope through Christ’s “eco-resurrection.” The course fosters an environmentally literate approach to preaching that engages congregational context—geography, culture, politics, and economics—and helps communities respond faithfully to the climate crisis with theological depth, prophetic imagination, and a commitment to justice for God’s Creation.


Prerequisite: LW 550
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Dr. Xavier Johnson
LW 592 - Practice Preaching for a Climate Challenged World
This course offers students an opportunity to develop and refine preaching skills focused on addressing the climate crisis and environmental justice. Building on foundational knowledge of Scripture, theology, and ecological issues, students will practice delivering sermons in a supportive, interactive online environment. Each participant will record and share a sermon, receive peer and instructor feedback, and engage in discussions that deepen their understanding of preaching’s role in a climate-challenged world. Through critical evaluation, sermon crafting, and spiritual reflection, students will enhance their ability to communicate biblical truths with theological integrity and pastoral sensitivity.

Note: This course meets synchronously on Zoom for four sessions. Each student will record themselves “practice preaching” one sermon and upload the video for fellow students and the instructor to watch. Each student will have one of the slots during the sessions to discuss their sermon and receive feedback.
LW 593 - Worship and Song Amid Climate Challenges
This course introduces students to an accessible means of proclaiming the gospel of ecological justice through Protestant worship, liturgy, and music. The weekly liturgies we practice and the music we sing as congregations form, inspire, teach, and shape us. They give communities faithful ways to lament, confess, pray, hope, and preach profoundly because we do these practices together—in unison and in harmony.
LW 670 – Interpreting and Preaching the Synoptic Gospels
Sound exegesis is necessary if today’s preaching is to contain any of the depth and power of the ancient Christian kerygma. The link between academic biblical scholarship and the life of the church and of the individual Christian sitting in the pew, however, is often strained. In this seminar students will enhance their skills in critical interpretation of the Synoptic Gospels that should be used in the service of preaching the Good News as well as examining pitfalls into which trained exegetes can fall when making the move from the desk to the pulpit.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LW 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LW 671 – Technology in the Sanctuary
This course examines the evolving role of technology in Christian worship and related ministries of the church, introduces students to theological and practical issues related to utilizing technologies available to worship planners, equip students with beginning skills in using some of these technologies, and gives chance for students to reflect on the influence technology has on their own spiritual lives.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LW 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LW 672 – Sermonic Design
During the last forty years, homiletical scholarship has given extensive attention to the question of sermonic form, especially since 1) content and form are inseparable and 2) sermon form implies a certain theological understanding concerning the nature of the Good News and of scripture, and vice versa. However, one rhetorical form does not fit all sermons. This course in sermonic design will serve as an introduction to a few of sermon forms that have been most influential over the last few decades, and will include discussions of how one chooses an appropriate form for a given sermon, how form shapes delivery, and how different forms are heard and experienced.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LW 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LW 673 – Preaching in Post Modernity
Challenges to the Enlightenment epistemology and suspicion of authority arose in the late Twentieth century and continue to influence society and the church today. This course will explore the dynamics of postmodernism and a number of different homiletical responses to it.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LW 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LW 674 – Generational Issues in Preaching and Worship
This course examines the distinctive worldviews of five generational cohorts—Silent Generation, Boomers, Gen X, Millennials, and Gen Z—and their implications for worship and preaching. Through readings, lectures, videos, and dialogue, students will explore how historical, cultural, and religious experiences shape faith expression. The course equips students to translate the gospel across generational lines, fostering worship that connects diverse communities with the Holy and supports their growth as disciples in today’s church.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LW 500 level work
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Faculty
LW 675- Courageous Preaching: Approaching Controversial Justice Issues in the Pulpit
This course equips students for prophetic preaching on social issues, balancing gospel proclamation with community-building. Grounded in scripture, theology, and homiletic theory, students will engage the “sermon-dialogue-sermon” process to foster public discourse and deepen congregational relationships. Post-class assignments include preaching two recorded sermons and facilitating one deliberative dialogue session. The course prepares students to preach with courage and contextual sensitivity, addressing pressing societal concerns while nurturing trust and transformation within their ministry settings.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed LW 554 and at least one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LW 500 level work. It is recommended that students have completed one course of Practice Preaching before taking this class.
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 676- Next Level Preaching: Rooted and Reaching
Sharpen and expand your skills for preaching to take your sermons to the next level. We will learn ways to deepen the scriptural and theological roots of our preaching, while creatively using story, imagery, and “creativity teams” in our congregations to connect with listeners in their context. Drawing on lessons from a diverse range of “teachers,” such as stand-up comedians, jazz musicians, poets, and story-tellers, we will practice techniques for preaching in ways that engage the listener, create a powerful experience of God’s justice and grace, and compel us to live the gospel in the world.

PLEASE NOTE: This course requires you to “practice preach” once and then preach in your congregation. Both sermons must be recorded and submitted along with a manuscript.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed LW 554 and at least one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LW 500 level work. It is recommended that students have completed one course of Practice Preaching before taking this class.
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 677- Witness and Testimony in Appalachia: Environment, Community, and Purple Zone Preaching
This course immerses students in the complex realities of Appalachia through a four-day experience in eastern Kentucky. Students will engage in pre-immersion study and on-site pastoral listening to explore environmental, economic, and social challenges—including classism, racism, and cultural stereotypes. Emphasizing contextual preaching, the course equips students to proclaim the gospel amid contentious issues with compassion and clarity. Each student will preach once in their congregation, integrating insights from this immersive learning journey.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed LW 554 and at least one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LW 500 level work. It is recommended that students have completed one course of Practice Preaching before taking this class.
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 678- Preaching as a Performance
This course equips students to preach with embodied presence, voice, and creativity. Emphasizing the use of imagery, metaphor, and performance techniques, students will build a homiletical toolbox for engaging and inspiring sermons. The course explores embodiment in relation to gender, race, and physicality, and includes strategies for preaching in online worship contexts. Students will participate in asynchronous learning and two synchronous videoconference workshops, developing sermons that are theologically rich, contextually aware, and fully embodied.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed LW 554 and at least one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LW 500 level work. It is recommended that students have completed one course of Practice Preaching before taking this class.
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Dr. Leah Schade
LW 679- Apocalyptic Preaching
This course reclaims apocalyptic texts as sources of hope and resilience for the church amid global crises. Students will explore historical exegesis and preaching strategies that draw on the courage and ethical integrity of biblical communities facing persecution and upheaval. Emphasizing faithful proclamation in tumultuous times, the course equips students to interpret apocalyptic literature creatively and pastorally, offering congregations guidance, encouragement, and a renewed vision of God’s promises in the face of fear and despair.

Prerequisite: Successfully completed LW 554 and at least one competency exercise and a minimum of 60% of LW 500 level work. It is recommended that students have completed one course of Practice Preaching before taking this class.
Credit: 2.0
Instructor: Drs. Leah Schade & Jerry Sumney
♦ Updated 6/2/26
SIS 540 - Discernimiento Crítico y Análisis Contextual
Este curso se estructura en cuatro partes fundamentales: Localización social, Pensamiento crítico, Lectura crítica y Declaración de tesis/Citación de fuentes. El objetivo principal es proporcionar a les estudiantes una introducción sobre cómo analizar los principales argumentos de una lectura, redactar una declaración de tesis efectiva, citar referencias de manera adecuada y discernir fuentes de autoridad. Al concluir el curso, los estudiantes habrán adquirido nuevas habilidades que les permitirán abordar lecturas críticamente, expresarse por escrito de manera efectiva y posicionarse de manera fundamentada en torno a los temas en discusión.

Prerequisite: *Required within the First 8 Hours of MTS-LS*
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
SIS 570 – The Three Rs of Seminary
This course aims to assist students in improving their capacity to do three things: research the existing conversation on a topic of interest, to read that conversation analytically, and to write their own views clearly and cogently. These are critical skills for success in seminary. They are also critical skills for ministry in the church during and after seminary.

Today many students who are preparing for ministry are coming back to school after an absence from formal academic work and academic writing. Many students come from careers where expectations about writing are different than for graduate work and ministry. The Three R’s course is designed to assist you in becoming better readers, writers, and researchers in those contexts.

Prerequisite: *Required within the First 8 Credit Hours*
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
SIS 571 – The Two Ps of Seminary: Prayer and Praxis
Students can feel alternately surprised, overwhelmed, disillusioned, and delighted by theological education. While each student’s experience is different, this course is designed to prepare you for the impact that seminary courses often have on the life of faith (prayer) and approach to ministry (praxis) so that you can flourish spiritually and practically throughout and beyond your educational program. Students will begin to build connections of collegiality and relational learning using a cohort model during the course.

Prerequisite: *Required within the First 8 Credit Hours*
Credit: 1.0
Instructor: Faculty
SIS 572 - La Fe en Práctica
Entrar al seminario teológico no es solamente un ejercicio intelectual o formativo en términos académicos. Es también una experiencia profundamente encarnada: involucra el cuerpo, la mente y el espíritu. Este curso introductorio prepara a los nuevos estudiantes para lo que pueden esperar en su formación teológica: desde desarrollar pensamiento crítico y escritura teológica rigurosa, hasta aprender a pensar teológicamente, cultivar la espiritualidad en diálogo con la intelectualidad, y participar en discusiones saludables dentro de una comunidad diversa.
♦ Updated 06-17-2025
DM 811 – Building the Capacity of the Reflective Practitioner
This course aims to augment students’ skill at several skills sets related to research: formulating research problems; finding, analyzing, evaluating, engaging, and citing resources related to those problems; formulating and arguing claims related to those problems in the context of the discussion encountered in the resources found; engaging in critical theological reflection related to those problems and claims. In so doing, the course also aims to develop in students an identity as researchers whose work contributes to on-going discussion at the frontiers of the practice of ministry.

Credit: 2.0 (Offered Online)
Instructor: Dr. Jonathan Barnes
DM 812 – Building Cultural Frameworks for Contemporary Contexts
This course provides students with an introduction to the basic theoretical concepts and methodological tools of cultural anthropology, and emphasizes the ways in which the discipline helps us interpret how diverse populations construct and enact meaning. The tools of anthropological analysis not only help us understand the “other”, but allow us to see our own culture with fresh eyes and perhaps discover our own cultural biases and assumptions.

Credit: 2.0 (Offered during On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Dr. Elaine Penagos
DM 813 – Building Congregational/Ministerial Frameworks for Contemporary Contexts
This course introduces students to ways of studying congregational contexts using several different frames. These include the frames of culture, ecology, and resources. Students will learn, respectively, how to study the distinct ways of being together that congregations invent and practice, how to see congregations as organisms in their social and religious environment, and how to inquire into what assets or ‘capital’ congregations have and what might be accomplished with them. By learning to interpret congregations through these different frames, students will thereby learn how to imagine ways that congregations might adapt and change.

Credit: 2.0 (Offered during On-Campus Intensives)
Instructor: Dr. Yara Gonzalez
DM 814 – Building Theological Frameworks for Contemporary Contexts
This course helps students build the capacity to reframe ministerial and larger contexts in light of theological and biblical traditions. Students will come to understand the way in which our own theological understandings are situated within wider cultural contexts. They will practice interpreting their surrounding culture through biblical and theological lenses. Finally, they will explore ways that theological and biblical interpretation can serve as practices that shape ministerial contexts.

Credit: 2.0 (Offered Online)
Instructor: Dr. Wilson Dickinson
DM 815 – Building Capacity for Transformative Ministries
Through this course students will explore the dynamics of working with established institutions or of creating new structures within communities for transformative ministry. The first half of this course will consider the resources available in established institutions, including ecclesial, parachurch, and others and the tensions that exist between ministries and those other established institutions. Special attention will be paid to the skill of grant writing. The second half will focus on the gifts and challenges that accompany working with local community members, with special attention paid to community organizing. Throughout the class students will consider the role that power plays in their local context, the tensions and opportunities inherent in, and tools and methods for navigating these fields.

Credit: 2.0 (Offered Online)
Instructor: Drs. Wilson Dickinson & Courtney Wiley-Harris
DM 890 – Writing the D.Min. Project
Students will study the classic theory and practice of adaptive change with attention to its application to congregational leadership. They will then learn two approaches to leading congregations through change: narrative work and Appreciative Inquiry. Finally, they will study leadership as a spiritual activity and learn ways to sustain themselves through the challenges of leading congregations through adaptive change.

Credit: 2.0 (Offered Online)
Instructor: Dr. Wilson Dickinson
DM 891 – Final Project
The final D.Min. project represents six credits of doctoral level work on a problem, issue or question in the ministry and mission of the church in the contemporary world that defines and evaluates an appropriate response to that problem, issue or question. The project will contribute new knowledge about the nature and practice of ministry in contemporary church and society at a level of significance that the student’s peers would want to see shared in professional contexts. The audience of the project is the student’s peers in ministry. The project will employ a reflection-action-reflection methodology, and use the approaches to cultural analysis, congregational analysis, theological reflection, and leadership through adaptive change developed in the program.

Credit: 6.0 (Offered Online)
Instructor: Dr. Wilson Dickinson
